question: what are faceted plots

sections.text: Faceted plots represent a fundamental concept in data visualization that enables the examination of data relationships across multiple dimensions or categories. This report explores the definition, theoretical foundations, implementation approaches, and applications of faceted plots in modern data visualization practices.

Faceted plots, also known as small multiples or conditioning plots, are a visualization technique that creates multiple subplots (panels) within a single graphic display, where each subplot shows a subset of the data conditioned on the values of one or more categorical variables (Hirsch et al., 2019). The concept of conditioning plots by the levels of one or more factors is called faceting, which fundamentally involves splitting data into subsets and displaying each subset in its own panel or subplot (Yin et al., 2021).In the context of the grammar of graphics framework, faceting represents one of the core layered components that can be specified when constructing visualizations. This component involves splitting plots based on categorical variables to create multiple panels, each displaying a different subset of the data (Kansal et al., 2021).

sections.text: ### Grammar of Graphics FrameworkFaceted plots are deeply rooted in Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics, which provides a structured framework for describing and constructing visualizations. Within this grammar, faceting constitutes one of the seven layered components: data, aesthetics, scale, geometric objects, statistics, facets, and coordinate system (Shang et al., 2024). The grammar treats faceting as a mechanism for partitioning datasets by categorical variables, creating a systematic approach to generating multiple related visualizations simultaneously.The layered grammar of graphics, as refined by Wickham, positions faceting as a critical component that enables the visualization of complex, multi-dimensional datasets by breaking them down into more manageable and interpretable subsets (Shang et al., 2024).### Generalized Faceting ConceptsRecent developments have expanded the traditional concept of faceting beyond simple categorical partitioning. Modern implementations allow faceting to be any mapping that transforms an input dataset into a collection of one or more subsets, where these subsets are not required to be exhaustive or mutually exclusive (Pagès et al., 2022). This generalization enables more sophisticated data analysis scenarios, including the creation of "all" categories alongside normal partitions and comparisons of particular categories against all observations.

sections.text: ### ggplot2 ImplementationThe ggplot2 visualization library provides two primary functions for creating faceted plots: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(). The facet_grid() function is capable of generating a 2D grid of graphics panels by column and/or by row, using formulas such as facet_grid(.~ group) for column-wise faceting or facet_grid(group ~ sex) for creating a 2D grid based on two categorical variables (Yin et al., 2021).In contrast, facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon of plots into a 2D arrangement, creating a string of panels that are "wrapped" into the graphics region. This function provides greater flexibility in controlling the arrangement of panels through parameters like ncol and nrow (Yin et al., 2021).### Advanced Visualization ToolsModern visualization tools have incorporated faceting capabilities with enhanced customization options. For example, specialized applications support multivariate data analysis through faceting, allowing users to map multiple variables using different aesthetic attributes while maintaining the faceted structure (Kapoor et al., 2023). These tools often provide options for setting axis scales to be either fixed across all facets or free to vary independently, depending on the analytical requirements.

These visualizations help analysts understand liquidity provision patterns across different market conditions and time periods (Hirsch et al., 2019).### Composite Plot CreationIn psychology and human neuroscience research, faceted plots support the creation of composite visualizations that combine multiple subplots into cohesive analytical displays. This approach accommodates the increasing sophistication of research involving multiple variables, conditions, and methodologies (Lin & Lu, 2023).

sections.text:
Topological Autoencoders represent a significant advancement in dimensionality reduction and manifold learning, combining the power of deep learning with topological data analysis. While traditional autoencoders excel at learning compressed representations of high-dimensional data, they often fail to preserve the global topological structure of the input space, leading to representations that may lose important geometric and topological relationships present in the original data.

Topological Autoencoders address this fundamental limitation by incorporating topological constraints directly into the learning process. The key innovation lies in using persistent homology, a technique from topological data analysis, to measure and preserve the multi-scale topological features of both the input and latent spaces during training [1]. This approach ensures that the learned low-dimensional representations maintain the essential topological structure of the original high-dimensional data.

citations.title: Topological Autoencoders

sections.text:
The theoretical foundation of Topological Autoencoders rests on persistent homology, which provides a mathematical framework for analyzing the topological structure of data across multiple scales. Persistent homology captures topological features such as connected components (0-dimensional features), loops (1-dimensional features), and higher-dimensional holes by constructing a sequence of simplicial complexes from the data [2].

The process begins with the construction of a Vietoris-Rips complex from a point cloud representation of the data. For a given dataset X, the Vietoris-Rips complex at scale ε includes all subsets of points whose pairwise distances are at most ε. As ε increases, a filtration is created - a nested sequence of simplicial complexes that captures the topological structure at multiple scales [3].

The persistent homology calculation tracks how topological features appear (birth) and disappear (death) as the scale parameter increases. Features that persist across a wide range of scales are considered significant topological characteristics of the data, while short-lived features are typically attributed to noise [4]. This multi-scale analysis is represented in a persistence diagram, which plots birth and death times of topological features.

sections.text:
A critical challenge in incorporating topological constraints into deep learning is the inherently discrete nature of topological computations, which makes backpropagation difficult. Topological Autoencoders solve this by developing a differentiable topological loss term that can be integrated into standard gradient-based optimization [5].

The key insight is that the persistent homology calculation can be viewed as a selection of topologically relevant edges from the distance matrix of the point cloud. Each persistence diagram entry corresponds to a specific distance between data points, and under the assumption that distances are unique (achievable through symbolic perturbations), the topological signature becomes differentiable [6].

sections.text:
A Topological Autoencoder follows the standard encoder-decoder architecture but incorporates an additional topological regularization term in the loss function. The encoder g: X → Z maps input data from the high-dimensional space X to a low-dimensional latent space Z, while the decoder h: Z → X reconstructs the original data [7].

The total loss function combines reconstruction error with topological preservation:
L_total = L_recon + λ·L_topo

where L_recon is the standard reconstruction loss (typically mean squared error), L_topo is the topological regularization term, and λ is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of topological constraints [8].

The topological regularization term L_topo compares the persistent homology of the input space with that of the latent space. The regularization works by tracking simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features. By consistently mapping these simplices to edges in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix. The topological loss then compares these "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space [10].

The analysis reveals that successful approaches combine both large-scale pretraining corpora and specialized fine-tuning datasets, with mathematical reasoning particularly benefiting from data augmentation techniques.

### 1.1 Core Training Datasets **MetaMathQA** stands out as one of the most effective specialized datasets for mathematical reasoning (Yu et al., 2023). This dataset contains 395,000 samples bootstrapped from GSM8K and MATH training sets, augmented using GPT-3.5 through multiple techniques: - Answer Augmentation (155k samples): Generates multiple reasoning paths for mathematical questions - Rephrasing (130k samples): Uses GPT-3.5 to rephrase questions while maintaining correctness - Self-Verification (55k samples): Converts questions into declarative statements with masked variables - FOBAR (55k samples): Backward reasoning approach starting from answers **MathInstruct** represents another significant dataset introduced by MAmmoTH, incorporating various mathematical problem datasets including GSM8K, MATH, AQUA, and Camel-Math (Yue et al., 2023). The dataset leverages GPT-4 to generate reasoning paths using both Program-of-Thought (POT) and Chain-of-Thought (COT) methods. **NuminaMath-TIR** has been used for domain-specific analysis, with research showing that algebra problems achieve the highest correctness rates while combinatorics presents the greatest challenge (Nikolaiev & Derevianchenko, 2024). ### 1.2 Data Augmentation Techniques **PersonaMathQA** introduces a novel persona-driven data augmentation approach, deriving enhanced datasets from MATH and GSM8K (Luo et al., 2024). Despite containing only 128.9K data points—32.6% of MetaMathQA and 49.5% of MathInstruct—models trained on this dataset achieve superior performance, demonstrating the importance of data quality over quantity. **SmallToLarge (S2L)** methodology reduces training data requirements significantly, achieving comparable performance with only 11% of the original MathInstruct dataset while maintaining 32.7% accuracy on the MATH benchmark (Yang et al., 2024).

## Introduction
Synthetic tabular data generation has emerged as a crucial technology for addressing contemporary challenges in data science, including privacy preservation, data scarcity, and data sharing limitations (Hansen et al., 2023). This technology has found widespread applications across various domains, particularly in highly regulated sectors such as healthcare and finance where traditional data sharing faces significant constraints (Potluru et al., 2023).

## Generative Model Approaches

### Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
Generative Adversarial Networks have been extensively adapted for tabular data generation. The Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) has emerged as one of the most prominent approaches in this domain (Gómez-Martínez et al., 2024). CTGAN utilizes a generator-discriminator architecture specifically designed to handle the complexities of tabular data, including mixed data types and discrete categorical variables (Ma et al., 2024).

Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of GANs for specific applications. Ma et al. (2024) showed that CTGAN could effectively enhance corrosion datasets for pipeline defect growth prediction, demonstrating superior performance compared to other data generation methods. Similarly, research has explored adapting image GANs for tabular data through novel transformation approaches, such as converting tabular instances into Two-Dimensional Feature Matrices (TDFMs) (Li et al., 2024).

However, GANs for tabular data face significant challenges. Miletic & Sariyar (2024) highlighted CTGAN's sensitivity to training parameters and noted scalability issues requiring substantial computational resources. Despite these limitations, GANs remain valuable tools for synthetic data generation when properly configured.

### Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
Variational Autoencoders represent another significant approach to synthetic tabular data generation. The Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE) has shown particular promise, demonstrating robustness across diverse datasets (Miletic & Sariyar, 2024). TVAE excels in high-dimensional data scenarios and maintains high utility across various datasets, though it incurs higher privacy risks due to the curse of dimensionality.

Recent innovations have combined VAEs with other techniques for enhanced performance. Appellaniz et al. (2024) proposed artificial inductive bias techniques for VAEs in data-scarce scenarios, achieving relative gains of up to 50% in synthetic data quality when using transfer learning and meta-learning approaches. Additionally, Stocksieker et al. (2024) developed methods combining VAE with smoothed bootstrap techniques specifically for imbalanced regression problems.

### Diffusion Models
Diffusion models have recently gained attention as a promising approach for tabular data generation. These models leverage denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to capture complex data distributions. Villaizán-Vallelado et al. (2024) proposed diffusion models with conditioning attention mechanisms, encoder-decoder transformers, and dynamic masking for both data imputation and generation tasks.

Several specialized diffusion approaches have been developed. Zhang et al. (2023) introduced Tabsyn, which combines diffusion models with VAEs in a latent space approach for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. Sattarov et al. (2024) presented FedTabDiff for federated learning scenarios, enabling collaborative training while preserving data privacy. The TimeAutoDiff model by Suh et al. (2024) specifically addresses time series tabular data by combining VAE and DDPM approaches.

## Privacy-Preserving Approaches

### Differential Privacy
Differential privacy has become a cornerstone technique for ensuring formal privacy guarantees in synthetic data generation. Sattarov et al. (2024) developed the DP-Fed-FinDiff framework, integrating differential privacy with federated learning and diffusion models for financial data. This approach demonstrates how privacy-preserving mechanisms can be successfully incorporated into generative models without completely compromising data utility.

### Federated Learning
Federated learning approaches enable synthetic data generation without centralizing sensitive data. The SiloFuse framework by Shankar et al. (2024) addresses cross-silo tabular data synthesis using distributed latent tabular diffusion architecture. This approach proves particularly valuable for scenarios where data features are distributed across multiple organizations while maintaining privacy constraints.

## Evaluation Frameworks and Metrics

### Comprehensive Evaluation Dimensions
The evaluation of synthetic tabular data has evolved to encompass multiple dimensions. Hernandez et al. (2022) established a three-dimensional evaluation framework covering resemblance, utility, and privacy aspects. This framework provides a standardized approach to assess synthetic data quality across different generation methods and datasets.

More recent work has expanded evaluation frameworks. Lautrup et al. (2024) introduced SynthEval, an open-source framework that treats categorical and numerical attributes equally without special preprocessing requirements. The framework integrates statistical and machine learning techniques for comprehensive evaluation of synthetic data fidelity and privacy-preserving integrity.

### Quality Assessment Metrics
Liu et al. (2024) emphasized the importance of comprehensive evaluation in learning analytics contexts, proposing evaluation criteria that balance privacy and data utility requirements. Their work demonstrates that synthetic data can maintain similar utility to real data while preserving privacy, though the selection of appropriate generation methods depends on specific application requirements.

## Applications and Use Cases

### Healthcare Applications
Healthcare represents one of the most significant application domains for synthetic tabular data. Rashidi et al. (2024) developed the Synthetic Tabular Neural Generator (STNG) specifically for healthcare data, incorporating multiple synthetic data generators with Auto-ML validation modules. This approach addresses the stringent regulatory requirements and data sensitivity concerns prevalent in healthcare settings.

### Financial Applications
The financial sector has embraced synthetic data for various applications due to regulatory constraints and privacy requirements. Potluru et al. (2023) provided a comprehensive overview of synthetic data applications in finance, covering tabular, time-series, event-series, and unstructured data modalities. The highly regulated nature of finance makes synthetic data particularly valuable for addressing privacy, fairness, and explainability concerns.

### Class Imbalance and Fairness
Synthetic data generation has shown promise in addressing class imbalance and fairness issues. Panagiotou et al. (2024) conducted comparative analyses of synthetic tabular data generation methods for addressing both class imbalance and group imbalances in protected attributes. Their results demonstrate the effectiveness of generative models for bias mitigation, creating new opportunities for fair machine learning applications.

## Challenges and Future Directions

### Data-Centric AI Integration
Hansen et al. (2023) highlighted the importance of integrating data-centric AI techniques to guide synthetic data generation processes. Their comprehensive benchmark study revealed that neglecting data profiles during generation can have significant consequences despite seemingly high statistical fidelity. This work emphasizes the need for more sophisticated approaches that consider data characteristics throughout the generation process.

### Inter-column Relationship Preservation
Long et al. (2025) identified preserving inter-column logical relationships as a significant challenge in current generative models. Their LLM-TabFlow approach leverages Large Language Model reasoning to capture complex inter-column relationships, representing the first explicit attempt to address this fundamental challenge in synthetic tabular data generation.

### Scalability and Computational Efficiency
Current synthetic data generation methods face significant scalability challenges. Research indicates that GANs require substantial computational resources, and the trade-offs between model complexity, generation quality, and computational efficiency remain areas requiring further investigation (Miletic & Sariyar, 2024).

sections.text: Based on my comprehensive search of the literature, I'll now generate a detailed report on the state-of-the-art work for 3D mesh generation from multi-view 2D images. # State-of-the-Art Work for 3D Mesh Generation from Multi-view 2D Images ## 1. Introduction 3D mesh generation from multiple 2D images has become a fundamental problem in computer vision and computer graphics, with applications ranging from virtual reality and augmented reality to robotics and autonomous navigation. The field has evolved significantly with the advent of deep learning and neural rendering techniques, leading to remarkable advances in reconstruction quality and efficiency. This report examines the current state-of-the-art approaches categorized by their underlying methodologies.

## 2. Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction ### 2.1 Neural Radiance Fields and Volume Rendering Approaches Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and related volume rendering techniques have revolutionized 3D reconstruction by providing continuous scene representations. **NeuS** represents a significant breakthrough in this domain by proposing to represent surfaces as zero-level sets of signed distance functions (SDFs) and developing a novel volume rendering method to train neural SDF representations (NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction). The method addresses the inherent geometric biases in conventional volume rendering and achieves high-quality surface reconstruction without mask supervision. Building upon NeuS, **Geo-NeuS** addresses the lack of explicit multi-view geometry constraints by directly locating the zero-level set of SDF networks and performing multi-view geometry optimization using sparse geometry from Structure from Motion (SfM) and photometric consistency (Geo-Neus: Geometry-Consistent Neural Implicit Surfaces Learning for Multi-view Reconstruction). This approach enables unbiased SDF optimization and focuses multi-view geometry constraints on true surface optimization. **Ref-NeuS** tackles the challenging problem of reconstructing reflective surfaces by utilizing an anomaly detector to estimate reflection scores and designing reflection-aware photometric loss functions (Ref-NeuS: Ambiguity-Reduced Neural Implicit Surface Learning for Multi-View Reconstruction with Reflection). ### 2.2 Enhanced Neural Surface Methods Recent advances include **Depth-NeuS**, which incorporates depth information optimization to improve reconstruction of objects with complex textures and color features (Depth-NeuS: Neural Implicit Surfaces Learning for Multi-view Reconstruction Based on Depth Information Optimization). **Res-NeuS** combines ResNet-50 with neural surface rendering for dense 3D reconstruction, introducing appearance embeddings and automatic sampling strategies for complex large-scale scenes (Res-NeuS: Deep Residuals and Neural Implicit Surface Learning for Multi-View Reconstruction).

question: What 2d barcode is resilient to compression?

sections.text:
## Executive Summary

Several 2D barcode symbologies demonstrate resilience to compression due to their robust error correction mechanisms. The most compression-resilient 2D barcodes are **QR codes**, followed by **Data Matrix** and **PDF417**, all of which utilize Reed-Solomon error correction codes that enable them to maintain readability even after image compression artifacts degrade their visual quality.

## QR Code Compression Resilience

QR codes are widely recognized as the most compression-resilient 2D barcode format. This resilience stems from their sophisticated error correction capabilities built on Reed-Solomon codes (He, 2025)¹. QR codes are known for their high data density and robust error correction capabilities, making them an ideal medium for secure data transmission even under compression conditions (He, 2025)¹. 

Multiple studies demonstrate QR codes' ability to withstand JPEG compression at various quality levels. Research shows that marked QR codes can perform well under JPEG compression with disparities of compression rates while maintaining decodability (cited in "A Puzzle-Based Data Sharing Approach with Cheating Prevention Using QR Code")². The robustness of QR codes to JPEG and JPEG2000 compression has been experimentally validated, with QR codes maintaining high visual quality and readability across different compression factors (cited in "Additional Information Delivery to Image Content via Improved Unseen–Visible Watermarking")³. 

The error correction capability of QR codes is preserved even when subjected to various forms of degradation, including compression artifacts. Studies demonstrate that QR codes can resist conventional attacks including rotation, resizing, JPEG compression of various quality levels, addition of salt-and-pepper noise and Gaussian noise (cited in "XOR-ed visual secret sharing scheme with robust and meaningful shadows based on QR codes")⁴.

## Data Matrix Compression Resilience

Data Matrix codes also exhibit significant compression resilience due to their Reed-Solomon error correction implementation. Research indicates that Data Matrix codes not only recover original data through error checking and correction algorithms even when damaged, but also maintain robustness against various attacks including JPEG compression, filtering and resizing (Kim et al., 2012)⁵.

A comprehensive study examining Reed-Solomon enabled bar code symbologies found that Data Matrix, along with QR codes, PDF417 and Aztec Code, achieved at least a 1 in 797 million error rate, demonstrating their capability for use in applications where decoded data accuracy is imperative even under compression conditions (cited in "Reed-Solomon Based Bar Code Character Substitution Rates")⁶.

## PDF417 Compression Resilience

PDF417 barcodes demonstrate robust compression resilience through their Reed-Solomon error correction system. PDF417 is described as a multi-row, variable-length symbology offering high data capacity and error-correction capability (cited in "Improving Performance of the Decoder for Two-Dimensional Barcode Symbology PDF417")⁷. The correction system is based on Reed-Solomon codes, similar to other resilient 2D barcode formats (cited in "2D Barcode for DNA Encoding")⁸.

Experimental evidence shows that PDF417 can handle significant degradation while maintaining decodability. In one study, a severely degraded PDF417 image with 42 erasures and 32 errors among 329 total codewords was still decoded correctly through Reed-Solomon error correction algorithms (cited in "Improving Performance of the Decoder for Two-Dimensional Barcode Symbology PDF417")⁷.

## Technical Foundation of Compression Resilience

The compression resilience of these 2D barcodes is fundamentally based on Reed-Solomon error correction codes. Reed-Solomon codes use forward error correction (FEC) support, which allows the barcodes to maintain functionality even when image compression introduces artifacts (cited in "Streaming QR Codes–A Survey")⁹. These codes can detect and correct multiple errors within the data, making them particularly effective against the types of degradation introduced by lossy compression algorithms.

The error correction capability varies by barcode type and configuration, but all three formats (QR codes, Data Matrix, and PDF417) utilize Reed-Solomon codes as their primary error correction mechanism, providing them with inherent resilience to compression-induced errors.

question: If you are a researcher currently thinking about an approach to whether transformers can be utilized to solve the problem of ranking fusion, where the information that can be obtained is hierarchically supervised information; are there any articles in the field of information retrieval where transformers have been used to solve or discuss this problem?

sections.text: This report examines the current state of research on utilizing transformers for ranking fusion problems in information retrieval, with particular emphasis on hierarchical supervised approaches. The analysis reveals several relevant research directions, though the specific combination of transformers, ranking fusion, and hierarchical supervision remains an emerging area with significant opportunities for novel contributions.

Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of combining transformer-based models with traditional ranking fusion techniques. Zhang et al. (2022) proposed a multi-dimensional ranking approach that utilizes pre-trained language models based on the transformer architecture fine-tuned on the MS MARCO corpus for usefulness assessment, combined with BERT-based models for supportiveness evaluation¹. The resulting ranked lists were combined using the Reciprocal Rank Fusion algorithm to obtain the final ranking of documents across multiple quality dimensions.Yu et al. (2023) introduced Fusion-in-T5 (FiT5), a novel re-ranker that integrates document text information, retrieval features, and global document information into a single unified model using templated-based input and global attention². This approach demonstrates how transformer architectures can be adapted to handle multiple ranking signals simultaneously through attention mechanisms, achieving significant improvements over traditional cascade systems.Deng et al. (2024) presented an industrial multimodal recommendation framework that employs transformers with a set of trainable queries to fuse different modalities and generate fixed-length multimodal embeddings³. Their approach utilizes Low-Rank Adaptation techniques to handle the computational complexity while maintaining effectiveness in ranking tasks.

Yoo et al. (2024) specifically addressed hierarchical supervision in ranking contexts by proposing a method that jointly performs summary and sentence-level supervision⁴. Their approach designed two sentence-level loss functions: intra- and inter-sentence ranking losses, demonstrating how hierarchical supervision can improve the learning of detailed and complex information in ranking models.The field has seen development in generalized weak supervision methods for neural information retrieval. Lien et al. (2023) proposed an iterative re-labeling process where weakly supervised models can iteratively serve as weak labelers⁵. This work suggests potential for hierarchical supervision where different levels of supervision can be automatically generated and refined.Li and Gaussier (2021) introduced KeyBLD, which employs hierarchical transformer architectures to build document-level representations on top of passage-level representations⁶. While not specifically focused on ranking fusion, this work demonstrates the feasibility of hierarchical transformer approaches in information retrieval contexts.

Recent research has explored decomposing transformer-based ranking into modular components. The development of modularized transformer-based ranking frameworks shows promise for incorporating hierarchical supervision at different architectural levels⁷. These approaches separate document representation, query representation, and interaction modules, providing multiple points where hierarchical supervision could be applied.Kong et al. (2024) proposed a retrieval-augmented generation method that combines ranking fusion with intent analysis⁸. Their approach uses semantic threshold optimization cleaning mechanisms based on ranking fusion, demonstrating how multiple levels of processing can be integrated in transformer-based systems.

citations.title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework

sections.text: Despite extensive research in transformer-based ranking and hierarchical supervision separately, there appears to be limited work that directly combines these approaches for ranking fusion problems. Most existing research either focuses on ranking fusion with traditional methods or applies hierarchical supervision in non-fusion contexts.Current transformer applications in ranking fusion primarily utilize standard attention mechanisms. There is significant opportunity to develop specialized hierarchical attention mechanisms that can leverage supervised hierarchical information more effectively.While reciprocal rank fusion and other traditional fusion methods have been combined with transformers, there is limited exploration of hierarchical fusion strategies that could benefit from transformer architectures' ability to model complex dependencies.

The literature reveals that while transformers have been successfully applied to both ranking fusion and hierarchical supervision problems independently, the specific intersection of these three areas (transformers + ranking fusion + hierarchical supervision) represents a significant research opportunity. Current work provides strong foundations in transformer-based ranking models, fusion techniques, and hierarchical supervision methods, but lacks comprehensive approaches that fully integrate all three components.For researchers considering this problem space, the existing literature suggests several promising directions: (1) extending modular transformer architectures to incorporate hierarchical supervision signals, (2) developing specialized attention mechanisms for hierarchical ranking fusion, and (3) creating end-to-end frameworks that can learn hierarchical representations while performing effective ranking fusion.The field appears ripe for innovative approaches that can leverage the representational power of transformers, the effectiveness of ranking fusion methods, and the guidance provided by hierarchical supervision to create more effective information retrieval systems.

question: Can LLMs learn new information when trained on supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?

sections.text: Research on whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can effectively learn new information through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reveals a complex picture. While LLMs can technically acquire new knowledge through fine-tuning, this process is significantly more challenging and less effective than utilizing pre-existing knowledge. The evidence suggests that LLMs primarily acquire factual knowledge during pre-training, with fine-tuning serving more to enhance the utilization of existing knowledge rather than meaningfully incorporating new information.

Recent empirical studies demonstrate that LLMs struggle to acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning. Research shows that "fine-tuning examples that introduce new knowledge are learned significantly slower than those consistent with the model's knowledge" (Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?). This finding indicates that while LLMs can eventually learn new facts, the process is substantially more difficult and time-consuming compared to reinforcing existing knowledge.Studies have found that "LLMs struggle to integrate new factual knowledge through fine-tuning" and that they "mostly learn to expose their pre-existing knowledge" rather than genuinely incorporating new information (Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?). This suggests that the apparent learning of new knowledge may be more superficial than genuine integration.Research indicates that when LLMs do appear to learn new facts through fine-tuning, they often engage in "mechanical memorization of fact statements" rather than developing deeper understanding (Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Beyond: A Comprehensive Survey on How to Make your LLMs use External Data More Wisely). Furthermore, "altering the phrasing of these memorized facts can render the recently learned knowledge ineffective, indicating a superficial level of understanding and retention by the LLMs."

citations.title: Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?

sections.text: A critical finding in the literature is that attempting to inject new knowledge through fine-tuning can lead to increased hallucinations. Research demonstrates that "as the examples with new knowledge are eventually learned, they linearly increase the model's tendency to hallucinate" (Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?). This creates a concerning trade-off where gaining new knowledge comes at the cost of reliability in existing knowledge.Studies show that "fine-tuning LLMs with new factual data may cause the models to mechanically memorize fact statements" and can "lead to a deterioration in the overall performance of the LLMs in generating accurate responses" (Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Beyond: A Comprehensive Survey on How to Make your LLMs use External Data More Wisely). This suggests that the process of knowledge injection through fine-tuning may be counterproductive to overall model performance.The literature reveals that "catastrophic forgetting is generally observed in LLMs ranging from 1b to 7b parameters" during continual fine-tuning (An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning). Moreover, "as the model scale increases, the severity of forgetting intensifies," indicating that larger models may be even more susceptible to losing previously acquired knowledge when learning new information.

Studies on "Injecting New Knowledge into Large Language Models via Supervised Fine-Tuning" demonstrate that "fact-based scaling offers a more systematic approach to ensure even coverage across all facts" and can lead to "considerable performance improvements in Q&A tasks related to out-of-domain knowledge" (Injecting New Knowledge into Large Language Models via Supervised Fine-Tuning).Innovative methods like "Self-Tuning" have been developed to improve knowledge acquisition by "augmenting the documents with a set of knowledge-intensive tasks created in a self-supervised manner, focusing on three crucial aspects: memorization, comprehension, and self-reflection" (Self-Tuning: Instructing LLMs to Effectively Acquire New Knowledge through Self-Teaching). This approach shows that "Self-Tuning consistently exhibits superior performance across all knowledge acquisition tasks and excels in preserving previous knowledge."Research suggests several strategies to minimize the negative effects of new knowledge injection:- Using early-stopping to "minimize the risk of the hallucinations caused by fitting the Unknown examples" (Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?)- Filtering out unknown examples to "substantially reduce the risk of overfitting, without sacrificing performance"- Incorporating "MaybeKnown fine-tuning examples, representing facts with lower degrees of certainty" to improve handling of uncertain information

While technically possible, the process is fraught with challenges including slow learning, increased hallucination risk, and potential performance degradation. The evidence strongly suggests that LLMs are primarily designed to acquire knowledge during pre-training, with fine-tuning serving to enhance the utilization of existing knowledge rather than meaningfully incorporating new information.For practical applications requiring up-to-date information, alternative approaches such as retrieval-augmented generation may be more effective than attempting to inject new knowledge through fine-tuning. When knowledge injection through fine-tuning is necessary, it should be approached with careful methodology, systematic validation, and appropriate mitigation strategies to minimize negative consequences.The field continues to evolve, with ongoing research into more effective methods for knowledge acquisition and retention in LLMs. However, the current evidence suggests that the most reliable approach is to ensure comprehensive knowledge acquisition during the pre-training phase, with fine-tuning reserved primarily for skill and behavior development.

question: how do GNNs perform on graphs with billions of nodes?

sections.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) face significant scalability challenges when applied to graphs with billions of nodes. The fundamental challenge lies in the exponential growth of computational and memory requirements as graph size increases (Sketch-GNN: Scalable Graph Neural Networks with Sublinear Training Complexity). Full-batch training on large graphs requires hundreds to thousands of gigabytes of memory, with datasets like MAG240M-LSC containing over 240 million nodes requiring more than 202 GB of GPU memory when fully loaded (Sketch-GNN: Scalable Graph Neural Networks with Sublinear Training Complexity).

The memory complexity for GNN training scales as O(m + ndL + d²L) on an n-node, m-edge graph with node features of dimension d when employing an L-layer graph convolutional network, making it difficult to train on graphs with millions of nodes or more due to GPU memory limitations (Sketch-GNN: Scalable Graph Neural Networks with Sublinear Training Complexity).

sections.text:
### 2.1 Memory and I/O Bottlenecks

The primary bottleneck in billion-scale GNN training is data movement between main memory and storage devices. Research shows that data movement between main memory and disk becomes the primary bottleneck in SSD-based training systems, with conventional GNN training pipelines being sub-optimal without accounting for this overhead (Ginex: SSD-enabled Billion-scale Graph Neural Network Training on a Single Machine via Provably Optimal In-memory Caching).

During graph sampling operations, nearly 48% of memory accesses are for graph structure (node IDs, edge offsets), and these accesses are small in size (8-64 bytes) and discontinuous, resulting in 100× smaller bandwidth utilization compared to large packages (Practical Near-Data-Processing Architecture for Large-Scale Distributed Graph Neural Network).

### 2.2 Computational Complexity Challenges

GNN training on billion-scale graphs involves both memory-intensive and computation-intensive operations that challenge current CPU/GPU platforms. The irregularity of graphs results in severe resource under-utilization and load-imbalance problems (GNNear: Accelerating Full-Batch Training of Graph Neural Networks with near-Memory Processing). The high byte-to-flop ratio makes aggregation operations memory and communication bandwidth bound rather than compute bound (DistGNN: Scalable Distributed Training for Large-Scale Graph Neural Networks).

### 3.1 Single-Machine Solutions

**SSD-Based Training Systems**: Ginex represents the first SSD-based GNN training system capable of processing billion-scale graph datasets on a single machine. By restructuring the GNN training pipeline and separating sample and gather stages, Ginex realizes Belady's algorithm for optimal caching of feature vectors, achieving 2.11× higher training throughput on average (2.67× at maximum) compared to SSD-extended PyTorch Geometric on four billion-scale graph datasets (Ginex: SSD-enabled Billion-scale Graph Neural Network Training on a Single Machine via Provably Optimal In-memory Caching).

**Bidirectional Propagation Methods**: The GBP (Graph Bidirectional Propagation) method achieves sub-linear time complexity for both precomputation and training phases, delivering superior performance on graphs with over 60 million nodes and 1.8 billion edges in less than half an hour on a single machine (Scalable Graph Neural Networks via Bidirectional Propagation).

### 3.2 Distributed Training Approaches

**Hybrid Parallelism**: The G3 system introduces GNN hybrid parallelism that synthesizes three dimensions of parallelism to scale out GNN training. G3 achieves up to 2.24× speedup in a 16-node cluster while maintaining better final accuracy over prior works on billion-edge graphs (Scalable and Efficient Full-Graph GNN Training for Large Graphs).

**Communication-Efficient Sampling**: FastSample addresses the sampling overhead in distributed environments, which becomes a significant component of training time for large-scale graphs. It achieves up to 2× speedup in distributed sampling-based GNN training with no loss in accuracy through novel graph partitioning and optimized sampling kernels (FastSample: Accelerating Distributed Graph Neural Network Training for Billion-Scale Graphs).

**Matrix-Based Bulk Sampling**: Advanced sampling techniques express sampling as sparse matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) and sample multiple minibatches at once, achieving 2.5× speedup over distributed PyTorch-Geometric extensions on 128 GPUs and 8.46× speedup on datasets outside of OGB (Distributed Matrix-Based Sampling for Graph Neural Network Training).

### 4.1 Real-World Deployment Performance

**Industrial Applications**: MacGNN has been successfully deployed to serve Taobao's homepage feed for over two months, providing recommendations for more than one billion users. The system addresses the computational complexity of aggregating billions of neighbors by introducing macro recommendation graphs that reduce neighbor counts from billions to hundreds while maintaining superior performance compared to twelve CTR baselines (Macro Graph Neural Networks for Online Billion-Scale Recommender Systems).

**WeChat Platform Deployment**: PlatoD2GL serves major traffic in WeChat Platform for training various GNN models, demonstrating up to 79.8% efficiency improvement and 6.3× improvement in time cost for dynamic graph topology updates (PlatoD2GL: An Efficient Dynamic Deep Graph Learning System for Graph Neural Network Training on Billion-Scale Graphs).

### 4.2 Benchmark Performance Metrics

**Training Speed Improvements**: DistGNN-MB achieves significant speedups on billion-scale graphs, training 3-layer GraphSAGE and GAT models on OGBN-Papers100M with epoch times of 2 seconds and 4.9 seconds respectively on 32 compute nodes. The system trains GraphSAGE 5.2× faster than DistDGL and achieves 10× and 17.2× speedup for GraphSAGE and GAT respectively when scaling from 2 to 32 nodes (DistGNN-MB: Distributed Large-Scale Graph Neural Network Training on x86 via Minibatch Sampling).

**Memory Efficiency**: Armada demonstrates runtime improvements up to 4.5× and cost reductions up to 3.1× on billion-scale graphs through disaggregated architecture and efficient partitioning algorithms (Armada: Memory-Efficient Distributed Training of Large-Scale Graph Neural Networks).

### 5.1 Sampling Bias and Accuracy Trade-offs

GNN-based models typically sample hundreds of neighbors out of billions to facilitate efficient online recommendations. However, sampling only a small portion of neighbors results in severe sampling bias and failure to encompass the full spectrum of user or item behavioral patterns (Macro Graph Neural Networks for Online Billion-Scale Recommender Systems).

### 5.2 Communication Overhead

In distributed settings, communication volume increases significantly because vertex feature vectors and parameter gradients must be communicated, creating pressure on communication networks that can become bottlenecks. The lower flops density and sequential nature of training operations make it challenging to overlap computation with communication, exposing communication time (DistGNN: Scalable Distributed Training for Large-Scale Graph Neural Networks).

### 5.3 Resource Utilization Challenges

Current systems demonstrate poor scalability due to large and interleaved computation dependencies in GNN training that cause significant overhead in parallelization methods (Scalable and Efficient Full-Graph GNN Training for Large Graphs). The irregular nature of graph data structures leads to resource under-utilization and load imbalance problems across distributed systems.

question: what are the latest methods to deal with temporal reasoning in llms?

sections.text: Temporal reasoning remains one of the most challenging aspects for Large Language Models (LLMs), requiring understanding of temporal concepts, relationships between events, and complex temporal logic. Recent research in 2024 has introduced several innovative approaches to enhance LLMs' temporal reasoning capabilities, ranging from architectural improvements and specialized training methods to novel prompting techniques and hybrid frameworks.

Recent work has focused on representing temporal information as structured graphs to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities. The TG-LLM framework (Xiong et al., 2024) introduces a novel approach where temporal graphs (TGs) serve as latent representations for temporal reasoning tasks^[Large Language Models Can Learn Temporal Reasoning]. This method adopts a two-stage approach: first, LLMs are fine-tuned to translate text into temporal graph representations, then they perform deliberate reasoning over these TGs using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) bootstrapping and graph data augmentation.The LLM-DA (Large Language Models-guided Dynamic Adaptation) method addresses temporal knowledge graph reasoning by leveraging LLMs to analyze historical data and extract temporal logical rules^[Large Language Models-guided Dynamic Adaptation for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning]. This approach introduces a dynamic adaptation strategy that updates LLM-generated rules with the latest events, ensuring that extracted rules incorporate recent knowledge and better generalize to future event predictions without requiring fine-tuning.

citations.title: Large Language Models Can Learn Temporal Reasoning

sections.text: The Timo model represents a significant advancement in building universal frameworks for temporal reasoning tasks^[Timo: Towards Better Temporal Reasoning for Language Models]. This approach systematically studies 38 temporal reasoning tasks and develops a foundation by leveraging mathematical datasets, combined with a self-critic temporal optimization method to enhance temporal reasoning capabilities without sacrificing general task abilities. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance at both 7B and 13B scales.Recent research has explored parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods specifically adapted for temporal reasoning. Chain of History (Luo et al., 2024) employs parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies to harmonize LLMs with temporal knowledge graph completion requirements^[Chain of History: Learning and Forecasting with LLMs for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion]. This approach focuses on learning structural information of pivotal nodes within historical chains while addressing challenges in comprehending reverse temporal logic.

citations.title: Chain of History: Learning and Forecasting with LLMs for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion

sections.text: The TimeToM framework introduces temporal space construction as a foundation for improving Theory of Mind capabilities in temporal contexts^[TimeToM: Temporal Space is the Key to Unlocking the Door of Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind]. This method constructs Temporal Belief State Chains (TBSC) for each character within temporal space, dividing beliefs into self-world and social world beliefs that align with different orders of temporal reasoning questions.RECIPE-TKG presents a lightweight framework that combines rule-based multi-hop retrieval for structurally diverse history with contrastive fine-tuning of lightweight adapters^[RECIPE-TKG: From Sparse History to Structured Reasoning for LLM-based Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion]. The approach includes test-time semantic filtering to iteratively refine generations based on embedding similarity, achieving up to 30.6% relative improvement in Hits@10 performance.

The Test of Time benchmark introduces novel synthetic datasets specifically designed to assess LLM temporal reasoning abilities across various scenarios^[Test of Time: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Temporal Reasoning]. This approach addresses limitations of real-world data that LLMs may have encountered during pre-training by creating controllable synthetic datasets that enable systematic investigation of problem structure, size, question type, and fact order impacts on LLM performance.LTLBench proposes a novel pipeline for constructing datasets to evaluate temporal reasoning ability by leveraging random directed graph generation, Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas, and NuSMV model checkers^[LTLBench: Towards Benchmarks for Evaluating Temporal Logic Reasoning in Large Language Models]. This benchmark consists of 2,000 temporal reasoning challenges and provides insights into the impact of increasing events and formula operators on reasoning complexity.

Recent work has identified the crucial role of mathematical abilities in temporal reasoning. Research shows that 19 out of 38 studied temporal reasoning tasks are directly related to mathematics, leading to approaches that first establish solid mathematical foundations before addressing pure temporal reasoning challenges^[Timo: Towards Better Temporal Reasoning for Language Models].Emerging methods shift towards program-aided approaches that employ Python code as intermediate logical steps instead of natural language for time-sensitive tasks^[Living in the Moment: Can Large Language Models Grasp Co-Temporal Reasoning?]. While these methods show effectiveness, they highlight the need for approaches that better leverage the inherent capabilities of LLMs rather than relying heavily on external tools.

The latest research in temporal reasoning for LLMs demonstrates significant progress across multiple dimensions: structural representations through temporal graphs, specialized training methodologies, advanced prompting techniques, comprehensive evaluation frameworks, and hybrid approaches. The field is moving towards more sophisticated methods that combine the strengths of different approaches while addressing fundamental challenges in temporal logic understanding and reasoning. Future work continues to focus on developing universal frameworks that can handle diverse temporal reasoning tasks while maintaining efficiency and interpretability.

question: is there a vad system designed with weighted finite state transducers and deep neural networks? how does it work

sections.text: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) is a fundamental component in speech processing systems that determines whether a given audio frame contains speech or non-speech content. Traditional VAD approaches often suffer from suboptimal performance due to independent processing stages and rule-based decision logic. Recent advances have explored the integration of deep neural networks (DNNs) with weighted finite state transducers (WFSTs) to create more robust and unified VAD frameworks.

Yes, there are VAD systems specifically designed with both weighted finite state transducers and deep neural networks. The most notable example is the system described by Mateju et al. (2016), which combines DNNs for frame-level speech/non-speech classification with WFST-based decoders for output smoothing [1].

In this hybrid approach, various Deep Neural Networks are first evaluated and trained on datasets containing speech, non-speech data, and artificially created mixed data at different Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) levels [1]. The key innovation lies in post-processing the DNN output using a decoder based on Weighted Finite State Transducers to smooth the frame-level decisions and reduce misclassification errors [1].

citations.title: Study on the Use of Deep Neural Networks for Speech Activity Detection in Broadcast Recordings

sections.text:
### Neural Network Component

The DNN component serves as the primary feature extractor and classifier. In the implementation by Mateju et al., the baseline speech/non-speech detector utilizes a deep neural network with binary output [1]. The network architecture consists of five hidden layers, each containing 128 neurons, with ReLU activation functions and mini-batch training of size 1024 over 15 epochs [1].

The input features are 39-dimensional log filter banks, and the input vector for the DNN has a length of 51, formed by concatenating 25 preceding frames, the current frame, and 25 following frames [1]. This context window approach allows the network to capture temporal dependencies in the speech signal.

### WFST Smoothing Decoder

The critical innovation lies in the WFST-based smoothing component that processes the DNN output. The baseline DNN classifier operates on individual frames independently, which often results in frequent transitions between speech and non-speech classifications that don't correspond to actual speech segment boundaries [1]. This leads to increased Word Error Rates during transcription as frames incorrectly marked as non-speech are omitted from processing [1].

The WFST smoothing system consists of two transducers implemented using the OpenFst library [1]. The first transducer models the input speech signal, while the second represents the smoothing algorithm with three states: an initial state (0) and two emission states (1 and 2) that output corresponding labels [1]. Transitions between the emission states are penalized by penalty factors P1 and P2, with values of 500 each, determined through experimental optimization [1].

The decoding process employs on-the-fly composition of the transduction and input models, treating the input as a linear-topology, unweighted, epsilon-free acceptor [1]. The system compares the shortest path in the resulting model with alternative hypotheses and marks paths with common output labels as final fixed output, while uncertain portions remain as temporary output [1].

citations.title: Study on the Use of Deep Neural Networks for Speech Activity Detection in Broadcast Recordings
Endpoint detection using weighted finite state transducer

sections.text:
### WFST-Based Endpoint Detection Framework

A broader framework for integrating VAD with WFSTs is presented by Chung et al. (2013), who propose a unified WFST-based endpoint detection system [2]. This approach addresses the fundamental problem that traditional endpoint detection systems consist of two cascaded but independent decision processes: frame-level VAD classification and utterance-level detection with state transition control [2].

The traditional approach suffers from several limitations: it requires expert knowledge to define rules, needs sophisticated implementation to avoid rule conflicts, and yields suboptimal performance because each process operates independently [2]. The proposed WFST-based framework integrates both processes into a single unified system, eliminating the need for separate rule-based logic at the utterance level [2].

### Integration Benefits

The experimental results demonstrate that integrating these two processes through the WFST framework allows the endpoint detection problem to be solved in a more straightforward manner [2]. This unified approach eliminates the suboptimal performance issues inherent in systems where VAD and utterance-level detection are handled separately [2].

citations.title: Endpoint detection using weighted finite state transducer

sections.text:
### Accuracy Improvements

The DNN-WFST hybrid system demonstrates significant improvements over standalone approaches. The WFST smoothing component leads to substantial improvement in the accuracy of DNN-based detectors, effectively reducing residual misclassified frames [1]. The system achieves a Frame Error Rate (FER) of 5.56% on broadcast data while missing close to 6% of speech frames, with significantly better performance on clean data (1.39% FER) [1].

### Computational Efficiency

Despite the additional WFST processing, the system maintains high computational efficiency. The final VAD module achieves a Real-Time Factor (RTF) of around 80, making its computational demands almost negligible [1]. This efficiency is crucial for real-time applications such as broadcast transcription systems.

### Transcription System Integration

When integrated into speech transcription systems, the DNN-WFST VAD approach provides dual benefits: the speech recognition accuracy remains comparable or even slightly better than systems without VAD, while significantly reducing computation time by preventing non-speech frames from being processed [1]. For example, a one-hour radio program containing advertisements, songs, and music can be trimmed to just a few utterances totaling several tens of seconds [1].

citations.title: Study on the Use of Deep Neural Networks for Speech Activity Detection in Broadcast Recordings

sections.text:
### Multi-condition Training

To improve robustness, the system employs multi-condition training using artificial data created by mixing clean speech and non-speech recordings at various SNR levels [1]. This approach extends the training dataset by adding recordings containing non-speech events such as music and jingles, addressing the limitation of clean-condition training data [1].

The artificial dataset creation process involves mixing 30 hours of clean speech with 30 hours of non-speech recordings, with volume adjustments to achieve desired SNR levels randomly chosen between -30 dB and 50 dB [1]. Labels are automatically generated based on SNR thresholds, with recordings above the threshold marked as speech [1].

### Optimization Results

Experimental evaluation shows that using mixed training data leads to significant improvements, with substantial reductions in both FER and Miss Rate (MR) across all threshold values [1]. The optimal SNR threshold of 5 dB provides the best balance for the target application, considering both speech detection accuracy and false alarm rates [1].

The unified framework approach eliminates the suboptimal performance issues of traditional cascaded systems and provides both improved accuracy and computational efficiency for practical applications such as broadcast transcription and endpoint detection.

question: planning with Large Language Models

sections.text: Planning with Large Language Models (LLMs) represents a rapidly evolving intersection of artificial intelligence where natural language processing capabilities meet automated reasoning and decision-making. Large language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization abilities in many domains, yet they face significant challenges when applied to long-horizon planning problems (Liu et al., 2023). Unlike classical planners that can efficiently solve formatted problems using search algorithms, LLMs struggle with the systematic reasoning required for optimal planning solutions. The field has emerged as researchers seek to leverage LLMs' natural language understanding capabilities while addressing their inherent limitations in logical reasoning and sequential decision-making. This convergence has led to innovative hybrid approaches.

citations.title: LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency

sections.text: ### 2.1 Hybrid LLM-Classical Planner Integration The most promising approach combines LLMs with classical planning systems. The LLM+P framework represents a pioneering effort that takes natural language descriptions of planning problems, converts them to Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), leverages classical planners for solution finding, and translates results back to natural language (Liu et al., 2023). This approach achieves optimal solutions for most benchmark problems while standalone LLMs fail to provide even feasible plans. Similarly, LiP-LLM integrates linear programming and dependency graphs with LLMs for multi-robot task planning, addressing key challenges in managing dependencies between skills and optimizing task allocation (Obata et al., 2024). This framework utilizes LLMs to generate comprehensive skill lists and construct dependency graphs while employing linear programming for optimal task allocation. ### 2.2 Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought Approaches LLM-Planner demonstrates effective few-shot planning for embodied agents, achieving competitive performance with recent baselines despite using less than 0.5% of paired training data (Song et al., 2022). The framework enhances LLMs with physical grounding to generate and update plans grounded in current environments. Chain-of-thought reasoning has emerged as a critical enhancement method. OR-LLM-Agent leverages Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning capabilities to translate natural language problem descriptions into formal mathematical models and automatically generate solver code (Zhang & Luo, 2025). Research has shown that chain-of-thought methods significantly enhance LLMs' ability to solve complex tasks through explicit intermediate inference (Cao et al., 2024). ### 2.3 Multi-Agent Collaborative Planning SMART-LLM introduces an innovative framework for multi-robot task planning that harnesses LLMs to convert high-level task instructions into multi-robot task plans through task decomposition, coalition formation, and task allocation stages (Kannan et al., 2023). The framework operates within the few-shot prompting paradigm and demonstrates promising results across both simulation and real-world scenarios. LLM-Collab presents a cooperative interaction framework between two AI agents, with one serving as an analyst for tool selection and phase validation, and another as an executor of specific tasks (Cao et al., 2024). This paradigm establishes a unified framework for autonomous task-solving based on language communication and tool selection.

question: Evaluating race biases in Large Language Models.

sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT, BERT, and LLaMA have transformed natural language processing, yet they exhibit social biases that can reinforce unfair outcomes¹. The evaluation of race biases in LLMs has become a critical concern as these models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications ranging from healthcare to hiring processes². Racial bias in LLMs can manifest in various forms, including stereotypical associations, differential treatment of racial groups, and systematic underrepresentation or misrepresentation of certain communities³.Recent research has identified that larger models exhibit superior performance but heightened biases, creating a performance-bias trade-off that complicates the deployment of fair AI systems⁴. The challenge is further compounded by the fact that these biases are often inherited from historical data patterns in training corpora, making them particularly insidious and difficult to detect⁵.

### 2.1 Template-Based Probing MethodsContemporary evaluation approaches employ template-based probing techniques to systematically assess racial bias⁶. These methods utilize standardized prompts with controlled variables to measure how models respond differently to racial identifiers while keeping other contextual factors constant⁷. This approach allows researchers to isolate racial bias from other confounding variables in model outputs.### 2.2 Established Bias BenchmarksSeveral key benchmarks have emerged for evaluating racial bias in LLMs:**CrowS-Pairs**: A crowdsourced dataset comprising 1,508 minimal pair sentences covering nine bias types, including race⁸. Each pair contrasts sentences about historically disadvantaged and advantaged groups, with crowd workers annotating the degree of stereotyping⁹. The dataset measures bias by comparing model preferences for stereotypical versus anti-stereotypical expressions.**StereoSet**: This benchmark evaluates model bias across four dimensions including race, using 17K instances of stereotypical bias annotated by crowd workers¹⁰. It employs a fill-in-the-blank methodology where models select from stereotypical, anti-stereotypical, or irrelevant words¹¹. The Idealized Context Association Test (ICAT) score combines language modeling performance with stereotype measurement.**WinoBias**: Originally designed for gender bias detection in co-reference resolution, this benchmark has been extended to evaluate racial associations with occupations and social roles¹².### 2.3 Statistical Evaluation MetricsResearchers employ various statistical metrics to quantify racial bias:- **Statistical Parity Difference (SPD)**: Measures the degree and direction of demographic bias by comparing representation rates across racial groups¹³- **Disparate Impact**: Assesses whether model decisions disproportionately affect certain racial groups¹⁴- **Equalized Odds**: Evaluates whether model performance metrics are consistent across racial groups¹⁵

Studies examining GPT-4, Claude-3, and Mistral-Large found significant racial biases in professional evaluation contexts, with different models showing varying preferences for racial groups¹⁶. For instance, Claude-3 and Mistral-Large generally favored Asian candidates, while GPT-4 preferred Black and Hispanic candidates in several specialties¹⁷.### 3.2 Healthcare Domain FindingsIn healthcare applications, racial bias manifests in particularly concerning ways. Research on performance status assignment revealed that models trained on race-specific data showed disparate classification results when applied to other racial groups¹⁸. Models tended to assign Black patients with initially favorable status (ECOG 0-1) worse performance ratings (ECOG 2+), highlighting potential for perpetuating healthcare disparities¹⁹.### 3.3 Long-Text Generation BiasThe Long Text Fairness Test (LTF-TEST) framework, covering 14 topics and 10 demographic axes including race, uncovered subtle biases in essay-style outputs that are difficult to detect in simple responses²⁰. The average Statistical Parity Difference across seven models showed -11.93% for Hispanic groups and -0.77% for Asian groups, indicating consistent underrepresentation²³.

sections.text: ### 4.1 Benchmark Reliability IssuesCurrent bias evaluation benchmarks face significant reliability concerns. The instability of model performance on CrowS-Pairs and StereoSet across different pre-training runs raises questions about the consistency of bias measurements²⁴. The small size of CrowS-Pairs (approximately one-fourth the size of StereoSet) contributes to high variability in results, particularly for underrepresented categories like religion with only 105 examples²⁵.### 4.2 Evaluation ParadoxA fundamental challenge in bias evaluation is the "random model paradox," where a random language model could achieve perfect stereotype scores of 50% on benchmarks like StereoSet, despite being functionally useless²⁶. This highlights that reduced bias scores might reflect degraded language modeling capability rather than genuine bias reduction²⁷.### 4.3 Limited Scope of Current MethodsMost existing bias evaluations focus on simple tasks like multiple-choice questions, potentially overlooking biases that emerge in complex scenarios like long-text generation²⁸. Additionally, the lack of multiclass and multimetric studies constrains investigation to binary-focused methods, limiting comprehensive understanding of nuanced racial bias patterns²⁹.### 4.4 Cultural and Contextual LimitationsCurrent benchmarks primarily reflect Western, English-speaking contexts, potentially missing culturally specific manifestations of racial bias. The automatic translation of bias benchmarks into multiple languages, while useful, may not preserve the cultural nuances essential for accurate bias detection across different linguistic and cultural contexts³⁰.

Counterfactual data augmentation has shown promising results, creating balanced datasets by generating alternative versions of training examples with different racial identifiers³¹. This approach helps ensure more equitable representation across racial groups in training data.### 5.2 In-processing MethodsDuring model training, several techniques have proven effective:**Adversarial Training**: This approach trains models to be unable to predict protected attributes like race, forcing them to learn representations that are less dependent on racial identifiers³². Research shows this can achieve up to 48% reduction in bias indicators with minimal accuracy trade-offs³³.**Fairness-aware Loss Functions**: These modify the training objective to explicitly penalize biased predictions, encouraging models to learn more equitable decision boundaries across racial groups³⁴.### 5.3 Post-processing TechniquesPost-processing methods modify model outputs to reduce bias:**FT-REGARD**: A fine-tuning approach that pairs biased prompts with neutral responses has shown effectiveness in reducing racial bias³⁵. This method addresses bias in generated content while maintaining overall model performance.**Output Calibration**: Techniques that adjust model confidence scores and decision thresholds for different racial groups to achieve more equitable outcomes³⁶.### 5.4 Alternative Training Paradigms**Federated Learning**: Research demonstrates that federated learning approaches can reduce racial bias by allowing diverse data sources to contribute to model training without centralized data sharing³⁷. This approach showed significant improvements in Disparate Impact scores, with one study reporting improvement from 6.42 to 1.66³⁸.**Multilingual Training**: Evidence suggests that multilingual training effectively mitigates bias compared to monolingual approaches, with multilingual models achieving both lower bias and superior prediction accuracy³⁹.
