question: how is AI being used in academic advising

sections.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming academic advising in higher education institutions worldwide. This integration represents a shift from traditional manual advising processes to data-driven, personalized support systems that can enhance student outcomes and institutional efficiency. AI applications in academic advising span three primary areas: chatbots and conversational agents for immediate student support, predictive analytics for identifying at-risk students and success patterns, and personalized recommendation systems for course selection and career pathways. While these technologies offer significant benefits including 24/7 availability, personalized guidance, and improved student retention, they also present challenges related to ethics, privacy, and the need for human oversight.

The landscape of higher education is undergoing a technological revolution, with artificial intelligence emerging as a transformative force in academic support services. Academic advising, traditionally dependent on human advisors' intuition and experience, is being augmented and in some cases supplemented by intelligent systems capable of processing vast amounts of student data to provide personalized guidance (Albinali et al., 2024). This transformation addresses longstanding challenges in academic advising, including advisor availability, administrative inefficiencies, and the need for more personalized student support at scale.

citations.title: A Systematic Literature Review of the Artificial Intelligence Role in Transformative Academic Advising: A Study of AI Applications in Higher Education

sections.text: AI-powered chatbots represent one of the most visible applications of artificial intelligence in academic advising. These systems provide students with immediate, 24/7 access to academic information and guidance. Chatbots can function as academic advisors by utilizing students' data relevant to their academic progress and constructing suggestions for which courses a student should take (Bilquise & Shaalan, as cited in literature review). The sophistication of these systems has evolved significantly, with some institutions implementing bilingual AI-driven chatbots that can respond to students' questions relevant to regulations and educational policies in multiple languages. Modern chatbot implementations integrate with institutional databases containing students' academic history, registration schedules, program requirements, and frequently asked questions. Unlike human advisors, these chatbots are available around the clock to respond to both general and personalized queries using students' academic data. They can also initiate proactive reminders about deadlines and personalized alerts such as high absence rates to ensure students stay on track academically. Large Language Models (LLMs) like Llama2 are being specifically fine-tuned for academic advising contexts. Research has shown that LLM-powered solutions in admission consulting can offer significant benefits to students, including enhanced data confidentiality and providing students with a higher level of comfort when seeking information related to their academic performance and scores (Aguila et al., 2024).

citations.title: Large Language Model in Higher Education: Leveraging Llama2 for Effective Academic Advising

sections.text: Predictive analytics has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming academic advising from a reactive to a proactive approach. These systems analyze historical student data to forecast academic outcomes and identify students at risk of academic failure or dropout. Georgia State University exemplifies this approach, using predictive analytics to track more than 800 risk factors of dropout, which contributed to raising their 6-year graduation rate from 32% in 2003 to 55% in 2018 while reducing graduation rate gaps between disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged students. The implementation of predictive analytics in academic advising allows advisors to shift their focus from compliance-based advising to student success-focused guidance. By analyzing patterns in academic datasets, these systems can identify groups of courses that should ideally be taken together and predict the likelihood of student success in specific courses. This data-driven approach enables advisors to explore more course options and develop suitable study plans with lower failure risk for each student. Predictive models utilize various data sources including student demographic information, aptitude data such as standardized test scores, and learning management system data to create comprehensive risk profiles. These models can forecast student grades and identify at-risk students early in their academic journey, allowing for timely interventions.

AI-driven recommendation systems represent a sophisticated application of machine learning in academic advising, providing personalized course and learning pathway suggestions based on individual student profiles. These systems analyze students' academic history, learning preferences, performance patterns, and career goals to suggest optimal educational trajectories. Course recommendation systems utilize various approaches including collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and hybrid methods to generate personalized suggestions. Some systems employ K-means clustering analysis to examine students' preferences regarding course selection and assess students' engagement through indicators such as learning duration, interaction frequency, and feedback frequency. Advanced systems can provide "Netflix-style" course recommendations that account for students' interests, program requirements, and past performance. The development of personalized learning pathways goes beyond simple course recommendations to encompass comprehensive academic trajectory planning. These systems consider curriculum requirements, course prerequisites, and students' individual needs to suggest optimal sequences of learning activities. Research has shown that personalized recommendation systems can achieve significant adoption rates, with some studies reporting that 41.43% of students utilized automatically generated recommendations for elective course selection.

AI-driven academic advising systems have demonstrated significant positive impacts on student support and retention rates. Studies involving 1,200 university students across three institutions with AI-powered advising platforms showed significant improvements in students' perception of guidance quality, timely decision-making, and clarity in career planning. Students reported increased satisfaction and a stronger sense of being academically supported, with many noting that AI-generated insights helped them make informed choices about courses and careers (Soomro et al., 2025). The continuous availability of AI systems addresses one of the traditional challenges in academic advising: advisor availability. Research indicates that reduced advisor availability has a significant impact on administrative efficiency, and AI systems can augment process flow while reducing reliance on human advisors. Higher administrative efficiency through AI implementation is directly related to students' preference for AI-based advising systems.

citations.title: AI-Driven Academic Advising in Higher Education: Leveraging Intelligent Systems to Personalize Student Support, Improve Retention, and Optimize Career Pathways

sections.text: AI systems enhance the quality of academic decision-making by providing evidence-based recommendations rather than relying solely on advisors' intuition and experience. Predictive analytics enables advisors to make data-driven decisions about course selections and academic pathways, improving students' likelihood of degree completion and success in their chosen fields. The implementation of AI in academic advising has led to measurable improvements in institutional outcomes. Beyond Georgia State University's success, other institutions have reported enhanced student engagement and academic performance through AI-powered tools that provide personalized advice and early warnings of poor performance.

The implementation of AI in academic advising raises significant privacy and data security concerns. AI systems require extensive collection and analysis of student data, including academic performance, learning patterns, behavioral information, and sometimes biometric data. This comprehensive data collection raises concerns, particularly when much of this data pertains to minors who may not fully understand the implications of their information being collected and analyzed. Educational institutions must implement robust security measures to protect sensitive student data and address questions about long-term storage and potential future uses of collected information. The principle of data minimization—collecting only data necessary for specific educational purposes—becomes crucial in this context. There are legitimate concerns about whether information collected about a student's learning difficulties or behavioral patterns could be used in ways that may disadvantage them later in life.

AI systems are only as unbiased as the data they are trained on and the humans who design them. In academic advising contexts where AI is increasingly used for high-stakes decisions such as course recommendations or academic pathway guidance, the potential for bias can have far-reaching consequences. question: are there any diversity based coreset selection algorithm that minimizes l2 distance?

sections.text: Coreset selection is a fundamental problem in machine learning and computational geometry that seeks to identify a small, representative subset of data points from a larger dataset while preserving essential geometric and statistical properties. The question of whether diversity-based coreset selection algorithms exist that specifically minimize L2 distance is particularly relevant for applications requiring Euclidean distance preservation and geometric accuracy.

The most prominent diversity-based coreset selection algorithm that operates with L2 distance is the **k-Center Greedy algorithm**. This method addresses the facility location problem by selecting k points that minimize the maximum distance from any point in the dataset to its nearest selected center (Chen et al., 2024)¹. The algorithm "treats a video as a mini-dataset and employs the K-Center-Greedy algorithm to compute the distances between frames" (Chen et al., 2024)¹. The k-Center Greedy algorithm formulates the problem as: selecting k samples from dataset T such that the largest distance between a data point in T\S and its closest data point in S is minimized (Chen et al., 2023)². This approach explicitly uses distance metrics, including L2 norm, to ensure diversity in the selected coreset.

Geometric coreset methods assume that "data points close to each other in the feature space tend to have similar properties" and employ distance-based selection criteria (Wang et al., 2023)³. These methods "try to remove those data points providing redundant information" by using geometric distance measures including L2 norm (Wang et al., 2023)³.

Several coreset selection methods can be "recast as a facility location problem characterized by the teacher model" where the objective "encourages the coreset to be representative of the entire population in a pairwise similarity sense" (Anonymous, 2023)⁴. These approaches utilize distance metrics, including L2 distance, to maximize diversity while maintaining representativeness.

Recent work has identified limitations in existing diversity-based coreset selection methods that rely on L2 norm. Wan et al. (2024) note that "existing methods typically measure both the representation and diversity of data based on similarity metrics, such as L2-norm" but argue that these approaches "fall short of adequately capturing diversity" (Wan et al., 2024)⁵. Their Contributing Dimension Structure method addresses these limitations while still operating within the L2 distance framework.

The RCS method "searches for an informative subset that minimizes a representational divergence, which is the distance of the representation between natural data and their virtual adversarial variants" (Xu et al., 2023)⁶. This approach employs distance minimization principles that can incorporate L2 distance metrics for diversity-based selection.

Ceccarello et al. (2020) developed "the first coreset-based algorithms for diversity maximization under matroid constraints for various diversity functions" where "diversity function [is] expressed in terms of pairwise distances, where distance models dissimilarity" (Ceccarello et al., 2020)⁷. Their approach provides a framework for diversity maximization that can utilize L2 distance as the underlying distance metric.

The k-Center Greedy algorithm, while NP-hard in its exact formulation, provides strong approximation guarantees when using L2 distance. The "greedy approximation known as k-Center Greedy has been proposed" as an effective solution to the minimax facility location problem (Chen et al., 2023)².

Many diversity-based coreset selection methods rely on submodular optimization principles. These methods utilize "submodular gains in feature space" where the objective is "to maximize the diversity between selected points and the selected set while minimizing the distance between selected points and the remaining set" (Anonymous, 2023)⁸.

Diversity-based coreset selection with L2 distance minimization has been successfully applied in active learning scenarios. The "CORESET: A diversity-based approach using coreset selection" method computes embeddings and selects "samples at each round using a greedy furthest-first traversal conditioned on all labeled examples" (Anonymous, 2021)⁹.

Recent applications demonstrate the effectiveness of L2-based diversity coreset selection in deep learning contexts. These methods have been integrated into neural network training pipelines where "the embedding of each example is computed by the network's penultimate layer" and diversity-based selection is performed using L2 distance metrics (Anonymous, 2021)⁹.

Yes, there are diversity-based coreset selection algorithms that minimize L2 distance. The most prominent example is the **k-Center Greedy algorithm**, which explicitly formulates the coreset selection problem as minimizing the maximum L2 distance from any data point to its nearest selected center. This algorithm and its variants provide strong theoretical guarantees and have demonstrated practical effectiveness across various applications including active learning, neural network training, and geometric data analysis. Additional methods such as the Contributing Dimension Structure approach, Robustness-Aware Coreset Selection, and general facility location-based frameworks also incorporate L2 distance minimization within diversity-based coreset selection paradigms. These algorithms balance the dual objectives of maintaining dataset diversity while minimizing reconstruction error measured in L2 norm.

sections.text: Genetic algorithms (GA) are powerful metaheuristic optimization techniques inspired by natural evolution. However, their performance heavily depends on proper parameter tuning and optimization strategies. This report provides evidence-based guidance on optimizing genetic algorithms for improved performance, convergence, and solution quality.

### 2.1 Population Size Optimization Population size is one of the most critical parameters affecting genetic algorithm performance. Research demonstrates that population size significantly impacts both convergence speed and solution quality. A study on missile trajectory optimization found that "crossover function and population size are observed as highly impacting parameter in missile trajectory optimization" (Parameter Optimization of Genetic Algorithm Utilizing Taguchi Design for Gliding Trajectory Optimization of Missile). Optimal population size selection requires balancing exploration and exploitation. Large population sizes maintain diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence but increase computational cost. Research on wear resistance design showed that "a population size of 40 provides a high global search capability (62.33) and a reasonable convergence time (3.67 s)" when compared to larger populations that showed decreased global search capability (Wear Resistance Design of Laser Cladding Ni-Based Self-Fluxing Alloy Coating Using Machine Learning). ### 2.2 Crossover and Mutation Rate Optimization The optimization of crossover and mutation probabilities is crucial for maintaining the balance between exploration and exploitation. Studies indicate that "when configuring the crossover probability (Pc) and mutation probability (Pm) in genetic algorithms, it is common to select a larger crossover probability, typically ranging from 0.5 to 1.0, while keeping the mutation probability within a smaller range of 0.001 to 0.05" (Wear Resistance Design of Laser Cladding Ni-Based Self-Fluxing Alloy Coating Using Machine Learning). Dynamic parameter adjustment has shown promising results. Research on dynamic parameter tuning suggests implementing adaptive strategies where "mutation ratio slowly increases and the crossover ratio decreases (MICD)" during runtime, particularly effective "when the size of the population was large" (A dynamic approach for parameter tuning in genetic algorithm using crossover and mutation ratios).

sections.text: Company name matching is a critical task in data integration, business intelligence, and financial analysis, particularly when dealing with heterogeneous datasets where organization names may appear in various formats, contain typos, or use different conventions. Traditional exact matching approaches are insufficient due to the inherent variations in company name representations. This report examines embedding-based approaches and complementary techniques for measuring company name similarity.

Traditional fuzzy string matching remains fundamental to company name similarity detection. The Levenshtein distance (edit distance) measures the minimum number of single-character edits required to transform one string into another¹. In company name matching applications, normalized Levenshtein distance is commonly used, where the distance is divided by the length of the longer string to account for varying name lengths¹. Research shows that normalized Levenshtein distances below 0.15 typically indicate good matches for company names, while distances below 0.3 suggest similar matches¹. Composition-based similarity measures include Jaccard similarity and cosine similarity². Jaccard similarity calculates the ratio of common characters to total characters, making it effective when typographical errors are rare. However, Levenshtein distance excels at identifying typos while Jaccard similarity performs better with character transpositions². The Jaccard distance for company names typically uses a threshold of 0.2 for good matches and 0.9 for similar matches¹. Research demonstrates that no single string similarity algorithm provides optimal performance across all scenarios². Advanced systems combine multiple algorithms using weighted ensemble methods, where individual algorithm outputs are aggregated with weights reflecting their reliability for specific applications². The Adaptive Fuzzy String Matching (AFSM) approach employs human-in-the-loop learning to generate bespoke string-distance measures tailored to each application².

sections.text: The foundations of language modeling can be traced back to the mid-20th century with the development of statistical approaches to language understanding. These models used statistical techniques to predict the next word in a sequence based on the previous n-1 words. The effectiveness of n-gram models relied heavily on various smoothing techniques to combat overfitting and handle unseen word combinations (Mezzoudj & Benyettou, 2018).### 2.2 Benchmarking ProgressThe development of standardized benchmarks was crucial for measuring progress in statistical language modeling. Chelba et al. (2013) introduced the "One Billion Word Benchmark," which provided a comprehensive corpus for evaluating language modeling techniques with almost one billion words of training data. This benchmark showed that baseline n-gram models achieved significant performance levels, with the unpruned Kneser-Ney 5-gram model achieving a perplexity of 67.6.

(2019) introduced BART, a denoising autoencoder for pre-training sequence-to-sequence models. BART generalized both BERT (due to its bidirectional encoder) and GPT (with its left-to-right decoder), demonstrating particular effectiveness when fine-tuned for text generation while also performing well on comprehension tasks (Lewis et al., 2019).

sections.text: ### 6.1 GPT EvolutionThe GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) series represents a landmark progression in autoregressive language modeling. sections.text: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) technologies has necessitated the development of new competence frameworks to guide individuals and organizations in effectively utilizing these powerful tools. This report examines the current landscape of generative AI competences frameworks, exploring their theoretical foundations, core components, implementation strategies, and policy implications. The analysis reveals a rapidly evolving field where traditional digital literacy frameworks are being expanded and adapted to address the unique challenges and opportunities presented by generative AI technologies.

The development of generative AI competences frameworks builds upon established digital literacy and AI literacy foundations. Traditional frameworks such as the Digital Competence Framework for Citizens (DigComp) have been adapted to address emerging technologies. Van Audenhove et al. This definition emphasizes the dynamic and ongoing nature of competency development in the rapidly evolving field of generative AI.

question: What benchmarks are there for language models reasoning and what is the state of the art

sections.text: This report examines the current landscape of benchmarks for evaluating reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs) and analyzes the state-of-the-art performance across different reasoning domains. The report covers mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and comprehensive evaluation frameworks, highlighting both achievements and ongoing challenges in the field.

Mathematical reasoning represents one of the most challenging and well-studied domains for language model evaluation. Several key benchmarks have emerged as standards for assessing mathematical capabilities.### 1.1 Core Mathematical Benchmarks**GSM8K** stands as one of the most widely used benchmarks for evaluating mathematical reasoning in language models. As noted in recent research, "most state-of-the-art models for example achieve over 94% accuracy on the GSM8K dataset" (Scheherazade: Evaluating Chain-of-Thought Math Reasoning in LLMs with Chain-of-Problems). This high performance indicates that GSM8K may be approaching saturation for current frontier models.**MATH** represents a more challenging benchmark focusing on competition-level mathematics. Research shows that while models perform well on GSM8K, they struggle significantly more with MATH problems. For instance, "MetaMath-7B model achieves 66.4% on GSM8K and 19.4% on MATH" (MetaMath: Bootstrap Your Own Mathematical Questions for Large Language Models), demonstrating the substantial difficulty gap between these benchmarks.### 1.2 State-of-the-Art PerformanceCurrent state-of-the-art performance varies significantly across mathematical reasoning tasks. "MetaMath-70B achieves an accuracy of 82.3% on GSM8K, slightly better than GPT-3.5-Turbo" (MetaMath: Bootstrap Your Own Mathematical Questions for Large Language Models). However, performance on more challenging benchmarks remains limited, with models achieving much lower scores on competition-level mathematics.Recent evaluations have shown that "reinforcement learning (RL) approaches yield only modest improvements - far below prior claims - and are prone to overfitting, especially on small-scale benchmarks like AIME24. In contrast, supervised finetuning (SFT) methods show consistently stronger generalization" (A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning: Pitfalls and Paths to Reproducibility).### 1.3 Multimodal Mathematical ReasoningThe field has expanded to include multimodal mathematical reasoning. "CMM-Math contains over 28,000 high-quality samples, featuring a variety of problem types (e.g., multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and so on) with detailed solutions across 12 grade levels from elementary to high school in China" (CMM-Math: A Chinese Multimodal Math Dataset To Evaluate and Enhance the Mathematics Reasoning of Large Multimodal Models).

sections.text: Logical reasoning evaluation focuses on formal reasoning capabilities, including deductive and inductive reasoning tasks.### 2.1 Key Logical Reasoning Benchmarks**ReClor** and **LogiQA** serve as the primary benchmarks for evaluating logical reasoning capabilities. Research demonstrates that "LogicLLM demonstrates its effectiveness through successful improvements on two logical reasoning benchmarks (ReClor and LogiQA-v2)" (Exploring Self-supervised Logic-enhanced Training for Large Language Models).**Multi-LogiEval** represents a comprehensive approach to logical reasoning evaluation, "encompassing multi-step logical reasoning with various inference rules and depths. Multi-LogiEval covers three logic types — propositional, first-order, and non-monotonic consisting of more than 30 inference rules and more than 60 of their combinations with various depths" (Multi-LogiEval: Towards Evaluating Multi-Step Logical Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models).### 2.2 Challenges in Logical ReasoningCurrent research reveals significant challenges in logical reasoning evaluation. Studies show that "LLMs could interpolate and memorize the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet they struggle with slight variations of these puzzles" (On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning). This highlights the distinction between genuine reasoning and pattern memorization.### 2.3 Advanced Logical Reasoning ApproachesRecent work has focused on theory-guided reasoning approaches. "IDOL achieves state-of-the-art performance on ReClor and LogiQA, the two most representative benchmarks in logical reasoning MRC" (IDOL: Indicator-oriented Logic Pre-training for Logical Reasoning), demonstrating improvements through structured logical indicators.

sections.text: Commonsense reasoning evaluation assesses models' ability to understand implicit world knowledge and make intuitive inferences.### 3.1 Established Commonsense Benchmarks**COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives)** remains a fundamental benchmark for commonsense causal reasoning. Research shows that "determining the plausibility of causal relations between clauses is a commonsense reasoning task that requires complex inference ability" (Improving Commonsense Causal Reasoning by Adversarial Training and Data Augmentation).**WinoGrande** represents another crucial benchmark for commonsense reasoning, focusing on pronoun resolution tasks that require world knowledge. Recent work establishing "new state-of-the-art on WinoGrande, CODAH, and CommonsenseQA" (G-DAug: Generative Data Augmentation for Commonsense Reasoning) demonstrates continued progress in this area.### 3.2 Comprehensive Commonsense Evaluation**RAINBOW** provides a multitask approach to commonsense evaluation. "UNICORN, that establishes new state-of-the-art performance across 8 popular commonsense benchmarks, aNLI (87.3%), CosmosQA (91.8%), HellaSWAG (93.9%), PIQA (90.1%), SocialIQa (83.2%), WinoGrande (86.6%), CycIC (94.0%) and CommonsenseQA (79.3%)" (UNICORN on RAINBOW: A Universal Commonsense Reasoning Model on a New Multitask Benchmark).### 3.3 Authoring and Generation ChallengesRecent research has explored LLMs' ability to create commonsense reasoning tasks. "LLMs that succeed in answering the original COPA benchmark are also more successful in authoring their own items" (From Test-Taking to Test-Making: Examining LLM Authoring of Commonsense Assessment Items), suggesting a correlation between reasoning ability and task generation capability.

sections.text: Modern language model evaluation requires holistic approaches that assess multiple dimensions of reasoning capability.### 4.1 BIG-Bench and BIG-Bench Hard**BIG-Bench** represents a comprehensive evaluation suite focusing on challenging tasks. "BIG-Bench (Srivastava et al., 2022) is a diverse evaluation suite that focuses on tasks believed to be beyond the capabilities of current language models" (Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them).**BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)** focuses on the most challenging subset of tasks. Research shows that "applying chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting to BBH tasks enables PaLM to surpass the average human-rater performance on 10 of the 23 tasks, and Codex (code-davinci-002) to surpass the average human-rater performance on 17 of the 23 tasks" (Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them).### 4.2 HELM Framework**HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models)** provides a standardized framework for comprehensive model evaluation. "We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of LMs. LMs can serve many purposes and their behavior should satisfy many desiderata" (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models). The framework evaluates models across multiple dimensions including accuracy, robustness, and fairness.### 4.3 Multimodal Reasoning Evaluation**Mementos** addresses sequential multimodal reasoning. We also employ a GPT-4 assisted method to evaluate MLLM reasoning performance" (Mementos: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Model Reasoning over Image Sequences). sections.text: Learning to rank (LTR) systems in information retrieval face significant challenges when learning from biased user interaction data, particularly click data. Click data contains various types of bias that can lead to suboptimal ranking models if not properly addressed. The primary challenge lies in the fact that user clicks are not unbiased indicators of document relevance, as they are influenced by factors such as document position, user trust in the system, and examination patterns.Unbiased learning to rank (ULTR) has emerged as a critical research area aimed at mitigating these biases to learn effective ranking functions from biased user feedback (Yu et al., 2023). The field recognizes that neural models trained directly on biased click data without proper debiasing techniques produce unsatisfactory results, particularly when dealing with severely biased datasets.

citations.title: Feature-Enhanced Network with Hybrid Debiasing Strategies for Unbiased Learning to Rank

sections.text: ### 2.1 Position BiasPosition bias is the most well-studied form of bias in click data, where items at lower ranks are less likely to be examined and clicked by users, regardless of their actual relevance (Oosterhuis, 2022). This bias occurs because users tend to examine search results from top to bottom, with decreasing probability of examination as position increases.Position bias creates a fundamental challenge where highly relevant documents at lower positions receive fewer clicks than less relevant documents at higher positions, leading to a systematic underestimation of the relevance of lower-ranked items.### 2.2 Trust BiasTrust bias represents another significant challenge where users are more likely to click on items at higher positions because they trust the ranking system, even when those items may not align with their true preferences (Agarwal et al., 2019). This bias leads to false positive clicks where users click on irrelevant documents at high positions due to their trust in the system's ranking.Vardasbi et al. (2020) proved that existing Counterfactual Learning to Rank (CLTR) methods, including those specifically designed to handle trust bias, fail to completely remove this type of bias. They demonstrated that Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) is fundamentally unable to correct for trust bias under non-trivial circumstances.### 2.3 Examination BiasExamination bias relates to the user's decision to examine a document, which is not directly observable in click data (Zhao et al., 2023). This creates complications for debiasing methods that need to separate the examination behavior from the actual relevance assessment. The challenge lies in estimating examination probabilities without direct observation of user examination behavior.

citations.title: Doubly Robust Estimation for Correcting Position Bias in Click Feedback for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Addressing Trust Bias for Unbiased Learning-to-Rank
Separating Examination and Trust Bias from Click Predictions for Unbiased Relevance Ranking

sections.text: ### 3.1 Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS)Inverse Propensity Scoring has been the predominant approach for addressing position bias in ULTR. The method works by estimating click propensities at each position and then reweighting the observed clicks to correct for bias (Hu et al., 2018). However, IPS-based methods suffer from high variance, particularly when propensity scores are small, as the corrections involve propensities in denominators.The Unbiased LambdaMART algorithm represents a significant advancement in pairwise learning-to-rank that can simultaneously conduct debiasing and ranker training using pairwise loss functions. This method jointly estimates biases at both clicked and unclicked positions while learning an unbiased ranker.### 3.2 Propensity Ratio Scoring (PRS)Wang et al. (2020) identified a critical limitation in traditional IPS approaches: while they correct bias in clicks, they ignore the bias caused by implicitly treating non-clicked documents as irrelevant. Their Propensity Ratio Scoring method provides treatments for both clicks and non-clicks, avoiding unnecessary pairwise comparisons between relevant documents and achieving lower variability than traditional IPS methods.### 3.3 Doubly Robust MethodsDoubly robust (DR) estimation has been introduced to ULTR to provide more robust debiasing with lower variance compared to IPS methods (Oosterhuis, 2022). The key innovation in DR methods for position bias is using expected treatment per rank rather than actual treatment, since user examination is not directly observable in click data.DR estimators provide more robust unbiasedness conditions than IPS approaches and demonstrate enormous decreases in variance, requiring several orders of magnitude fewer data points to converge to optimal performance. This makes DR methods particularly valuable for practical applications where training data may be limited.### 3.4 Affine CorrectionsAffine correction methods generalize IPS to handle both position bias and trust bias simultaneously (Vardasbi et al., 2020). These methods both reweight clicks and penalize items displayed at ranks with high trust bias. The affine correction approach is proven to remove the effects of both trust bias and position bias, making it a more comprehensive solution than pure IPS methods.

citations.title: Doubly Robust Estimation for Correcting Position Bias in Click Feedback for Unbiased Learning to Rank
When Inverse Propensity Scoring does not Work: Affine Corrections for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Unbiased LambdaMART: An Unbiased Pairwise Learning-to-Rank Algorithm

sections.text: ### 4.1 Decomposed Ranking Debiasing (DRD)The Decomposed Ranking Debiasing approach addresses the high variance problem inherent in traditional propensity-based methods (Zhao et al., 2023). Instead of directly modifying clicks, DRD decomposes each click prediction into a relevance term from the ranking model and separate bias terms. This decomposition allows for learning unbiased relevance models with lower variance while maintaining unbiasedness.DRD employs a joint learning algorithm that alternately learns relevance and bias model parameters, providing theoretical guarantees of lower variance compared to existing methods while retaining unbiasedness properties.### 4.2 Mixture-Based Correction (MBC)Vardasbi et al. (2021) proposed mixture-based correction as an alternative approach that doesn't rely on relevance estimation, addressing the cyclic dependency issues in traditional methods. Introduction and DefinitionGrokking is a phenomenon where neural networks achieve perfect or near-perfect generalization on test data long after they have already achieved perfect performance on training data (Fan et al., 2024). This delayed generalization occurs after an extended period of overfitting, during which the network perfectly fits the training set but shows poor performance on unseen data. The term "grokking" was first introduced by Power et al. (2022) and has since become a significant area of research in understanding neural network training dynamics.The phenomenon is characterized by a sharp rise in generalization accuracy that occurs "tenfolds of iterations after near perfect overfitting to the training data" (Lee et al., 2024). This counterintuitive behavior challenges traditional understanding of machine learning, where generalization typically occurs early in training before overfitting begins.

sections.text: ## 2. Key Characteristics and Mechanisms### 2.1 Training DynamicsGrokking exhibits distinct training dynamics that differentiate it from conventional learning patterns. The phenomenon involves two distinct timescales in parameter updates: "the fast-varying, overfitting-yielding component and the slow-varying, generalization-inducing component" (Lee et al., 2024). This dual-timescale behavior explains why generalization occurs much later than the initial overfitting phase.Research has identified four distinct learning phases in grokking: "comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion" (Liu et al., 2022). The study found that representation learning occurs only in a "Goldilocks zone" between memorization and confusion phases, with the grokking phase staying closer to the memorization phase compared to the comprehension phase.### 2.2 Underlying MechanismsSeveral mechanisms have been proposed to explain grokking:**Feature Learning and Representation**: The transition from overfitting to generalization is "completely determined by feature learning" (Mallinar et al., 2024). Networks gradually learn structured representations, such as block-circulant features in modular arithmetic tasks, which enable generalization.**Complexity Dynamics**: Recent work suggests that grokking involves "a consistent pattern in training dynamics, consisting of a rise and fall in complexity" (DeMoss et al., 2024). This corresponds to memorization followed by generalization, viewed through the lens of Kolmogorov complexity.**Weight Dynamics**: The relationship between weight norms and grokking has been extensively studied, though recent research challenges "the prevalent hypothesis that the L2 norm of weights is the primary cause of grokking" (Golechha, 2024).

question: Summarise for me how kubernetes works and its difference to containers

sections.text: This report examines the fundamental architecture and operational principles of Kubernetes, and clarifies its relationship to container technology. While containers provide application virtualization, Kubernetes serves as a comprehensive orchestration platform that manages containerized applications at scale (Marella, 2024). The analysis reveals that Kubernetes and containers serve complementary rather than competing roles in modern cloud-native architectures.

Container technology represents a lightweight form of virtualization that packages applications with their dependencies into portable, isolated environments. According to Silva et al. (2024), "Container-based virtualization has received attention, especially with Docker, as an alternative, which also facilitates continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD)." Containers differ from traditional hypervisor-based virtualization by sharing the host operating system kernel while maintaining application isolation.Container technology offers several key advantages over traditional virtual machines. Silva et al. (2024) demonstrate that containers exhibit "low overhead and scalable performance" with reduced resource consumption compared to full virtualization solutions. The research shows that container deployment is "a longer and resource-intensive process" when using virtual machines, making containers more suitable for microservices architectures where rapid deployment and scaling are critical.

Kubernetes operates on a master-slave architectural model with distinct node types serving specific functions. As explained in the research, "Kubernetes follows the Master-Slave model, and nodes are divided into two roles: Master and Worker" (Zeus: Improving Resource Efficiency via Workload Colocation for Massive Kubernetes Clusters, 2024).### 2.1 Master Node ComponentsThe master node serves as the control plane for the entire Kubernetes cluster. According to the architectural analysis, the master node contains four critical components:- **Etcd**: A distributed key-value database that stores all cluster configuration and state data- **Kube-apiserver**: Provides the RESTful interface and serves as the single entry point for all cluster operations- **Kube-controller-manager**: Embeds core control loops that regulate the system state- **Kube-scheduler**: Continuously selects pending pods from the queue and assigns them to appropriate nodes based on resource availability### 2.2 Worker Node ComponentsWorker nodes execute the actual application workloads within the cluster. Research indicates that "Worker nodes are where applications execute within a pod" (Evolution and Trends of Cloud on Industrial OT Networks, 2024). Each worker node contains three essential components:- **Kubelet**: The primary node agent responsible for monitoring and managing all containers on the node- **Kube-proxy**: A network proxy that enables Kubernetes service abstraction and handles cluster networking- **Container runtime**: Responsible for container creation and management (commonly Docker or containerd)

question: Did anyone worked on aligning legal judgement predictions to human experts?

sections.text: Yes, several researchers have worked on aligning legal judgment predictions to human experts. This area of research has gained significant attention in recent years, with multiple approaches being developed to ensure that AI systems in legal contexts align better with human expert reasoning and judgment. The research encompasses various aspects including deconfounding models, expert evaluation frameworks, human-in-the-loop systems, and interpretability enhancement methods.

The most direct work on this topic is the research by Santosh et al. (2022), which specifically addresses the challenge of aligning legal judgment prediction systems with expert rationales¹. Their study demonstrates that Legal Judgment Prediction systems without expert-informed adjustments can be vulnerable to shallow, distracting surface signals that arise from corpus construction, case distribution, and confounding factors¹. To address this, they use domain expertise to strategically identify statistically predictive but legally irrelevant information and adopt adversarial training to prevent the system from relying on it¹. The researchers evaluate their deconfounded models by employing interpretability techniques and comparing them to expert annotations¹. Their quantitative experiments and qualitative analysis show that the deconfounded model consistently aligns better with expert rationales than baselines trained for prediction only¹. They further contribute a set of reference expert annotations to the validation and testing partitions of an existing benchmark dataset of European Court of Human Rights cases¹.

sections.text: Several researchers have developed comprehensive datasets with expert annotations to facilitate better alignment between AI systems and human legal experts. Sesodia et al. (2025) introduced AnnoCaseLaw, a first-of-its-kind dataset of 471 meticulously annotated U.S. Appeals Court negligence cases². Each case is enriched with comprehensive, expert-labeled annotations that highlight key components of judicial decision making, along with relevant legal concepts². Their dataset lays the groundwork for more human-aligned, explainable Legal Judgment Prediction models². Nigam et al. (2024) introduced PredEx, the largest expert-annotated dataset for legal judgment prediction and explanation in the Indian context, featuring over 15,000 annotations³. This groundbreaking corpus significantly enhances the training and evaluation of AI models in legal analysis³. Through rigorous lexical, semantic, and expert assessments, their models effectively leverage PredEx to provide precise predictions and meaningful explanations³. Another significant contribution comes from research on creating expert evaluation metrics. Studies have introduced human evaluation metrics such as "Clarity" and "Linking" to assess the quality of AI-generated judgment predictions and explanations⁴. These metrics are vital because while models may produce accurate predictions, their explanations often lack coherence or fail to justify the decision meaningfully⁴.

sections.text: Research has also focused on the broader aspects of human-AI collaboration in legal decision-making. (2024) examine the integration of Artificial Intelligence into judicial decision-making processes, focusing on the balance between technological assistance and human consideration of justice⁶. question: how the AI hallucination is linked to the AI bias

sections.text: AI hallucination and AI bias are interconnected phenomena that represent two of the most significant challenges in artificial intelligence systems today. Research reveals that these issues share common root causes in training data, model architecture, and statistical learning processes, while also reinforcing each other in complex ways that compromise AI system reliability and fairness.

AI hallucination refers to the phenomenon where artificial intelligence systems generate outputs that appear plausible and coherent but are factually incorrect or ungrounded in the input data (Halperin & Lukin, 2024). In text-to-image models, hallucination manifests as "generative hallucination" where models produce content that diverges from the intended prompt (Vice et al., 2025). AI bias encompasses various forms of systematic errors or unfairness in AI outputs, including statistical bias in training data, demographic bias affecting different population groups, and algorithmic bias arising from model architecture and training processes (Mensah, 2024).

sections.text: Both hallucination and bias often stem from problems in training data. Statistical bias in training datasets creates conditions that lead to both biased outputs and hallucinated content (Vice et al., 2025). When training data contains incomplete, biased, or contradictory information, models learn to generate outputs that reflect these flaws, manifesting as both hallucinations and biased responses (Huo & Johnson, 2025). Research shows that when there is divergence between source content and reference outputs in training data, it contributes to both hallucination and bias propagation. This phenomenon has been quantified in text summarization tasks, where intrinsic bias in training correlates strongly with extrinsic hallucination rates (Spearman correlation of 0.81-0.83) (Anonymous, 2024). The fundamental probabilistic nature of large language models makes both hallucination and bias inherent limitations rather than occasional glitches. When learned probability distributions are biased, incomplete, or overly general, models produce outputs that are statistically probable but factually incorrect or biased (Anonymous, 2025).

question: The difference between cross-language summarization and multilingual summarization

sections.text: Text summarization has evolved significantly with the advent of neural networks and transformer models, extending beyond monolingual approaches to encompass multilingual and cross-lingual paradigms (Wang et al., 2022). These two approaches represent distinct methodologies for handling summarization tasks across different languages, each with its own characteristics, challenges, and applications. Understanding the fundamental differences between cross-language summarization and multilingual summarization is crucial for researchers and practitioners working in natural language processing.

sections.text: Cross-language summarization (CLS), also referred to as cross-lingual summarization, is defined as "a process of generating a summary in the target language from a source document in another language" (Abka et al., 2022). More specifically, "given a document in a source language, cross-lingual summarization (CLS) aims to generate a summary in a different target language" (Wang et al., 2022). This task involves taking input documents in one language and producing summaries in a completely different language. The fundamental characteristic of cross-lingual summarization is that "document D_L and summary S_L' are in different languages L and L'" (Urlana et al., 2023). This approach enables the rapid dissemination of relevant content across speakers of different languages, such as providing summaries of English news articles to Czech or German speakers (Huot et al., 2023).

sections.text: Multilingual summarization represents a broader paradigm that encompasses multiple language capabilities within a single framework. According to recent research, multilingual summarization involves "monolingual and cross-lingual summarization from D_{L1,L2,...,Ln} to S_{L1,L2,...,Ln} within a single model" (Urlana et al., 2023). In contrast to cross-lingual approaches, multilingual systems "can handle the input-output pairs in the same language across several different languages" (Khanal et al., 2019). The key distinction is that multilingual summarization can perform both monolingual summarization (same language input and output) and cross-lingual summarization within a unified architecture. As one survey notes, "Multi-language summarization involves generating summaries for documents in various languages, but the output summary is in the same language as the input document. For instance, if the input is in French, the summary will be in French, if the input is in Japanese in the same model, the summary will be in Japanese" (Rahman et al., 2024).

sections.text: The most fundamental difference lies in the language handling capabilities. Cross-lingual summarization specifically focuses on language transfer, where "the cross-lingual summarization systems operate on input-output pairs that are not necessarily in the same language" (Khanal et al., 2019). This approach is inherently bidirectional or unidirectional between specific language pairs. Multilingual summarization, however, offers broader language coverage within a single model architecture. Research indicates that "monolingual and cross-lingual models could be more accurate as they concentrate on one language (pair), whereas multilingual models can significantly save storage and computational resources, and likely transfer knowledge across languages" (Urlana et al., 2023). Cross-lingual summarization faces "the compounded challenge of having to tackle difficulties relating to both monolingual summarization (e.g., long inputs and outputs, hallucinations) and machine translation (e.g., data imbalance, alignment across languages)" (Huot et al., 2023). Traditional approaches have relied on pipeline methods, either "first summarizing the source document and then translating the summary to the target language" or "translating the source document to the target language and then generating a summary" (Rahman et al., 2024). Multilingual summarization systems must address different challenges, primarily related to handling multiple languages simultaneously while maintaining quality across all supported languages. Recent work has shown that "multilingual transformer models, specifically mBART and mT5" have been successfully adapted for this purpose (Dhakal & Baral, 2024). The architectural approaches differ significantly between the two paradigms. Cross-lingual systems often employ specialized architectures like the "Cross-Attention Reinforcement (CAR) module" that "formulates a pseudo summarization policy parameterized by the cross-attention weights reinforced by the ground-truth monolingual summary" (Cai & Yuan, 2024). Multilingual systems typically leverage large-scale multilingual models that can handle multiple languages within a single architecture, as demonstrated by datasets like "PMIndiaSum, a multilingual and massively parallel summarization corpus focused on languages in India" with "196 language pairs" (Urlana et al., 2023).

question: When performing the HHL algorithm how does the solution use previous time step solutions to advance the solution in time?

sections.text: The research question contains a fundamental misconception about the HHL (Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd) algorithm. The HHL algorithm does not inherently use previous time step solutions to advance solutions in time in the traditional sense of iterative time-stepping methods. Instead, the HHL algorithm is primarily designed to solve static linear systems of equations Ax = b, where time evolution concepts are used internally as part of the quantum mechanical implementation, not as part of an iterative time-stepping procedure for differential equations.

The HHL algorithm is fundamentally a quantum algorithm for solving linear systems of equations Ax = b (Shwetha et al., 2025). The algorithm achieves an exponential speedup over classical methods for certain classes of problems, particularly when dealing with sparse and well-conditioned matrices (Tsemo et al., 2024). The algorithm operates through three main phases: quantum phase estimation to find eigenvalues of matrix A, controlled rotations to invert these eigenvalues, and uncomputation to obtain the solution state |x⟩ (Shwetha et al., 2025). Crucially, this is a direct solution method for linear systems, not an iterative time-stepping approach.

sections.text: When time evolution appears in the HHL algorithm, it refers to the quantum mechanical simulation of unitary operators, specifically the implementation of e^{iAt} where A is the coefficient matrix (Research on Quantum Computing Acceleration of Support Vector Machines in Multi-dimensional Nonlinear Feature Spaces, 2024). This time evolution is approximated through discrete controlled rotation gates, where each gate application represents a discrete time step dt in the quantum simulation. The time evolution operator e^{-iAt} is approximately realized by controlled revolving gates, which can only be approximated through a series of discrete operations (Research on Quantum Computing Acceleration of Support Vector Machines in Multi-dimensional Nonlinear Feature Spaces, 2024). The approximation involves breaking down the continuous evolution into discrete time steps, but this is for implementing the quantum algorithm itself, not for solving time-dependent problems iteratively.

sections.text: When the HHL algorithm is applied to solve differential equations, it typically involves discretizing the differential equation into a linear system and then solving that system directly (Kumar & Wilmott, 2024). For time-dependent problems, each time step requires solving a separate linear system, but the HHL algorithm itself does not carry forward previous solutions within its internal operation. For example, when solving the heat equation using quantum methods, researchers have employed quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) methodologies that track the scale of the state vector over time, but this is distinct from the standard HHL approach (Kumar & Wilmott, 2024). These specialized quantum algorithms for differential equations represent extensions or alternatives to HHL rather than applications of the basic HHL algorithm.

citations.title: Generalising quantum imaginary time evolution to solve linear partial differential equations

sections.text: Some researchers have developed iterative improvement methods for the HHL algorithm where previous solutions are used to refine accuracy (An Iterative Improvement Method for HHL algorithm for Solving Linear System of Equations, 2023). In these hybrid approaches, the solution from one HHL execution is used as input to improve the next iteration: x_m = y_m - x_m, where y_m is the solution obtained by HHL and x_m is a shift vector. However, this iterative refinement occurs at the classical post-processing level, not within the quantum HHL algorithm itself. The HHL algorithm in each iteration still solves the linear system directly rather than using time-stepping methods (An Iterative Improvement Method for HHL algorithm for Solving Linear System of Equations, 2023).

sections.text: For problems that genuinely require time evolution with dependence on previous solutions, researchers have developed alternative quantum algorithms. These include probabilistic imaginary-time evolution (PITE) operators for solving advection-diffusion equations, where the quantum state evolves through discrete time steps using information from previous states (Huang et al., 2024). The Koopman-von Neumann formalism represents another approach that maps nonlinear dynamics to Hilbert space where dynamics become unitary, effectively reducing differential equation problems to Hamiltonian time evolution (Barthe et al., 2023). These methods genuinely use time evolution with state progression, unlike the standard HHL algorithm.

The algorithm is designed to solve static linear systems directly through quantum phase estimation and controlled rotations. When time evolution concepts appear in HHL, they relate to the quantum mechanical implementation of unitary operators rather than iterative solution advancement. For problems requiring genuine time-stepping with dependence on previous solutions, alternative quantum algorithms like QITE or Koopman-von Neumann-based methods are more appropriate than the standard HHL algorithm.

question: how to improve chunk retrieval with contrastive learning?

sections.text: Chunk retrieval has become a cornerstone of modern information retrieval systems, particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications. The effectiveness of chunk retrieval largely depends on the quality of learned representations that can accurately capture semantic relationships between queries and document chunks. Contrastive learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving these representations by learning to distinguish between positive and negative examples in the embedding space. This report examines various strategies and techniques for enhancing chunk retrieval performance through contrastive learning approaches, focusing on recent advances in dense retrieval methods, hard negative mining, and contextual representation learning.

### 2.1 Core PrinciplesContrastive learning in retrieval systems operates on the principle of learning discriminative representations by maximizing similarity between semantically related query-document pairs while minimizing similarity with irrelevant pairs. The most commonly used objective function is the InfoNCE loss, which has been widely adopted in dense passage retrieval (DPR) systems (Tamber et al., 2025).The standard contrastive loss formulation involves comparing all pairs of queries and passages in a batch, where given a query embedding q, the corresponding gold passage embedding p_t, and passage embeddings p_i, the loss function aims to maximize the inner products of embeddings between queries and their relevant passages (Karpukhin et al., 2020).### 2.2 Limitations of Conventional ApproachesRecent research has revealed significant limitations in conventional contrastive learning approaches for retrieval. Tamber et al. (2025) found that "fine-tuning using the conventional InfoNCE contrastive loss often reduces effectiveness in state-of-the-art models," highlighting the need for more sophisticated training strategies.The primary challenges include:- Coarse Query Positioning: Queries are only optimized to align with documents, leading to anisotropic query embedding spaces (Li et al., 2021)- Limited Negative Sampling: In-batch negative sampling reduces the number of negatives available for training, limiting the model's discriminative power- Context Neglect: Traditional methods encode passages independently, overlooking crucial contextual information from the broader document structure

sections.text: ### 3.1 Hard Negative MiningHard negative mining has emerged as a crucial technique for improving contrastive learning effectiveness. The fundamental principle is that "hard negatives play an important role in contrastive learning to maintain a strong gradient signal while randomly sampling negative features is incapable of generating strong gradient signals" (MixCSE, 2021).#### 3.1.1 Selection StrategiesEffective hard negative selection involves several strategies:1. Similarity-Based Selection: Using cosine similarity to identify negatives that are challenging but not false positives2. Dynamic Negative Mining: Continuously updating the pool of hard negatives during training based on current model performance3. Filtered Hard Negatives: Removing negatives with cosine similarity higher than 0.95 to positive passages to avoid false negativesThe GRITHopper approach demonstrates that "mining difficult hard negatives is essential for achieving good dense retrieval performance," selecting 10 hard negatives for contrastive loss and incorporating the most difficult one into generative loss (GRITHopper, 2024).#### 3.1.2 Multi-Positive Contrastive LearningTraditional contrastive learning uses single positive samples, but multi-positive approaches can significantly improve performance. The multi-positive contrastive loss is formulated as:L_multi = -log(Σ_{x+ ∈ X+} exp(f(x, x+)) / (Σ_{x+ ∈ X+} exp(f(x, x+)) + Σ_{x- ∈ X-} exp(f(x, x-))))This approach "benefits from all the available positives" and increases the discriminative performance of retrieval models.### 3.2 Contrastive Dual LearningThe DANCE (Contrastive Dual Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor) framework addresses the limitation of anisotropic query embedding spaces by incorporating dual training objectives. This approach "learns more tailored representations for queries and documents to keep the embedding space smooth and uniform" (Li et al., 2021).The dual learning paradigm includes:- Primary Objective: Standard document retrieval task- Dual Objective: Query retrieval task inspired by query likelihood- Embedding Space Optimization: Concentrating query embeddings closer to document representations while making document distributions more discriminative

sections.text: ### 4.1 The Context ProblemA critical limitation of modern document retrieval methods is that they "typically encode passages (chunks) from the same documents independently, often overlooking crucial contextual information from the rest of the document that could greatly improve individual chunk representations" (Conti et al., 2025).### 4.2 In-Sequence Negative Training (InSeNT)The InSeNT approach addresses contextual limitations through a novel contrastive post-training method combined with late chunking pooling. The UncertaintyRAG method employs a contrastive learning strategy where:L_contrastive = -log(exp(f(ch_i, ch_i+)) / (exp(f(ch_i, ch_i+)) + exp(f(ch_i, ch_i-)) + Σ_j exp(f(ch_i, ch_j))))This formulation considers anchor chunks, positive chunks, hard negative chunks, and remaining negative chunks from the current batch, providing more nuanced similarity calculations through inner product operations on BERT embeddings.

sections.text: Multimedia document adaptation has become increasingly important in today's heterogeneous computing environment where content must be delivered across diverse devices, networks, and user contexts. The proliferation of mobile devices, varying network conditions, and diverse user preferences necessitate sophisticated adaptation mechanisms to ensure optimal multimedia content delivery and user experience (Saighi et al., 2017). sections.text: Context-Aware Adaptation Mechanisms Context-aware adaptation represents one of the most significant paradigms in multimedia document adaptation. Current multimedia documents can be accessed anytime and anywhere with a wide variety of mobile devices, such as laptops, smartphones, and tablets, making platform heterogeneity, users' preferences, and context variations require document adaptation according to execution constraints (Dromzée et al., 2013). Traditional context modeling languages often fail to handle real-life user constraints, typically listing multiple information values that are interpreted by adaptation processes to deduce implicitly such high-level constraints. Recent research has addressed these limitations by proposing novel context modeling approaches based on services, where context information is linked according to explicit high-level constraints (Dromzée et al., 2013). These approaches utilize semantic Web technologies by specifying RDF profiles and experimenting on their usage across several platforms. Hybrid Adaptation Architectures A significant advancement in multimedia document adaptation is the development of hybrid approaches that combine multiple adaptation categories. In pervasive systems, contextual constraints can hinder the smooth execution of multimedia documents, leading to several adaptation approaches that operate as client-side, server-side, proxy-based, or peer-to-peer applications (Ayadi et al., 2025). Most traditional approaches rely on centralized mechanisms that adapt content at a single point, which introduces significant drawbacks related to resource overhead. The hybrid approach efficiently combines multiple adaptation categories such as client-side, server-side, proxy-based, and peer-to-peer to alleviate their limitations, with the main objective of improving the quality of service in adaptation processes (Ayadi et al., 2025). This approach enables self-reconfiguration by seamlessly switching from one adaptation category to another, depending on the computation context of users and device capabilities.

sections.text: The evolution of weights during transformer training represents a critical yet underexplored aspect of deep learning. Understanding these dynamics is essential for explaining the impressive capabilities of large language models and improving training efficiency. This report synthesizes recent research on weight evolution patterns, training dynamics, and parameter trajectories in transformer architectures.

Recent research has revealed that transformer training exhibits distinct phases with different weight evolution patterns. Yang et al. (2024) discovered that gradient flow serves as an inherent mechanism that naturally divides the training process into two phases in their analysis of shallow transformers¹. In Phase 1, the linear MLP quickly aligns with target signals for correct classification, while the softmax attention remains almost unchanged. In Phase 2, the attention matrices and the MLP evolve jointly to enlarge the classification margin and reduce the loss to a near minimum value¹. A novel property of gradient flow dynamics in transformers has been identified as "automatic balancing of gradients," which enables loss values of different samples to decrease almost at the same rate¹. This mechanism facilitates the proof of near minimum training loss and provides insights into the inherent regularization properties of transformer training dynamics¹. Tian et al. (2023) provided a mathematically rigorous analysis of 1-layer transformer training dynamics, revealing that self-attention acts as a discriminative scanning algorithm⁴. Starting from uniform attention, the model gradually attends more to distinct key tokens for specific next tokens to be predicted, while paying less attention to common key tokens that occur across different contexts⁴. This process follows a "scan and snap" dynamic, where attention weights progressively drop following the order of low to high co-occurrence between key and query tokens⁴.

sections.text: Saponati et al. (2025) presented a mathematical framework to analyze self-attention matrices by deriving the structures governing their weight updates⁵. Their research demonstrates that bidirectional training induces symmetry in the weight matrices, while autoregressive training results in directionality and column dominance⁵. These findings have been validated across multiple transformer models including ModernBERT, GPT, LLaMA3, and Mistral, spanning different input modalities such as text, vision, and audio⁵. The evolution of attention entropy during training has been identified as a crucial indicator of training stability. Zhai et al. (2023) tracked attention entropy for each attention head during training, which serves as a proxy for model sharpness⁶. They identified a common pattern where low attention entropy is accompanied by high training instability, which can manifest as oscillating loss or divergence⁶. This pathologically low attention entropy, corresponding to highly concentrated attention scores, was termed "entropy collapse"⁶. To address entropy collapse issues, spectral normalization techniques have been proposed. The research shows that attention entropy decreases exponentially fast with the spectral norm of the attention logits, providing motivation for spectral control approaches⁶. These methods successfully prevent entropy collapse in attention layers, promoting more stable training dynamics⁶.

sections.text: Zhou et al. (2023) proposed TempBalance, a layer-wise learning rate method based on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) Theory⁷. This approach characterizes the implicit self-regularization of different layers in trained models and demonstrates the efficacy of using HT-SR-motivated metrics to guide the scheduling and balancing of temperature across all network layers during training⁷. Research on weight dynamics in normalized networks has revealed how disparities in effective learning rates (ELRs) across layers evolve over time. Ali Mehmeti-Göpel and Wand (2023) formalized how these disparities evolve by modeling weight dynamics through the evolution of expected gradient and weight norms⁸. They proved that when training with any constant learning rate, ELR ratios converge to 1, despite initial gradient explosion⁸. The research identified a "critical learning rate" beyond which ELR disparities widen, which depends only on current ELRs⁸. This finding has led to the development of hyperparameter-free warm-up methods that successfully minimize ELR spread quickly in both theory and practice⁸.

sections.text: Shou et al. (2025) introduced Gradient Flow Matching (GFM), a continuous-time modeling framework that treats neural network training as a dynamical system governed by learned optimizer-aware vector fields⁹. By leveraging conditional flow matching, GFM captures the underlying update rules of optimizers such as SGD, Adam, and RMSprop, enabling smooth extrapolation of weight trajectories toward convergence⁹. Unlike black-box sequence models, GFM incorporates structural knowledge of gradient-based updates into the learning objective, facilitating accurate forecasting of final weights from partial training sequences⁹. The framework generalizes across neural architectures and initializations, providing a unified approach for studying optimization dynamics and accelerating convergence prediction⁹. The training process can be interpreted as a trajectory in network space—a time series of networks—where the training algorithm represents a dynamical system in graph space. Danovski et al. sections.text: Reversible data hiding vector quantization (RDH-VQ) represents a significant advancement in steganography and data security, combining the efficiency of vector quantization compression with the capability to embed and extract secret data while maintaining complete reversibility (Wang et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2022). This field has emerged as a critical research area due to the growing need for secure data transmission and storage in cloud computing environments and multimedia applications.Vector quantization is a lossy data compression technique widely used in image processing, where an image is divided into non-overlapping blocks and each block is represented by the index of the most similar codeword in a trained codebook (Cao et al., 2022). The integration of reversible data hiding techniques with VQ compression allows for the embedding of secret information while maintaining the ability to perfectly reconstruct the original data after extraction.

sections.text: The VQ encoding process involves several key steps: the original uncompressed image is first divided into a series of non-overlapping blocks, typically of size n 7n (Cao et al., 2022). For each image block, Euclidean distances between the block and all L codewords in the trained codebook C are calculated, and the index of the codeword with the minimum distance is recorded in the index table T. During decoding, the indices are used to reconstruct the image blocks using the corresponding codewords from the codebook.Traditional data hiding methods in VQ-compressed images operate on the VQ index table, embedding secret data by modifying the indices while preserving the visual quality of the reconstructed image (Qin et al., 2015). However, recent advances have introduced novel approaches that work directly with VQ codebooks rather than index tables, providing greater flexibility and embedding capacity (Wang et al., 2023).The reversibility aspect ensures that after extracting the hidden data, the original VQ-compressed image can be perfectly reconstructed without any distortion, which is crucial for applications requiring complete data integrity such as medical imaging and legal documentation.

This method embeds secret data into the compressed VQ index by checking whether the parity of the candidate SOC index matches the current embedding bit. When the parity matches and the encoding error remains below a predetermined threshold, the method achieves significant compression advantages.Recent developments have focused on reversible data hiding in encrypted VQ-encoded images, addressing privacy protection requirements in cloud storage scenarios (Cao et al., 2022). These schemes typically employ stream cipher and permutation techniques to encrypt both the codebook and index table, ensuring that image content remains protected while allowing authorized users to embed and extract secret data.Advanced schemes incorporate vector quantization prediction techniques combined with parametric binary tree labeling (PBTL) to optimize embedding capacity (Xu et al., 2021). These methods leverage the predictive capabilities of VQ compression to identify optimal embedding locations while maintaining high image quality after reconstruction.

question: LLM to synthesize material recipe for quantum dot led

sections.text: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in materials science represents a transformative approach to accelerating materials discovery and synthesis optimization. This report examines the current state and potential of using LLMs specifically for synthesizing material recipes for quantum dot Light-Emitting Diodes (QD-LEDs), an emerging display technology with significant commercial potential.Quantum dot LEDs have gained substantial attention due to their superior color purity, high brightness, and tunable emission wavelengths compared to conventional organic LEDs¹. However, the optimization of synthesis parameters for quantum dots remains a complex, multi-dimensional challenge that traditionally requires extensive experimental trial-and-error approaches². The integration of LLMs into this process offers unprecedented opportunities to streamline materials discovery and accelerate the development of high-performance QD-LEDs.

Recent developments have demonstrated the effectiveness of LLM-based frameworks for quantum dot materials development. A novel framework leveraging large language models has been proposed to optimize experimental procedures for synthesizing quantum dot materials with multiple desired properties³. This framework integrates synthesis protocol generation models and property prediction models, both fine-tuned on open-source large language models using parameter-efficient training techniques with in-house synthesis protocol data.The framework operates through a multi-step process where synthesis protocols with target properties and masked reference protocols are generated, followed by validation through property prediction models and assessments of novelty and human evaluation³. Empirical validation has confirmed the effectiveness of this LLM-driven approach, with synthesis experiments demonstrating that among six synthesis protocols derived from the framework, three successfully updated the Pareto front, and all six improved at least one property.LLMs have shown remarkable capability in predicting synthesis pathways for inorganic materials, including quantum materials⁴. Advanced frameworks contain three specialized models: LHS2RHS (predicting products from reactants), RHS2LHS (predicting reactants from products), and TGT2CEQ (generating full chemical equations for target compounds). Fine-tuning on text-mined synthesis databases has resulted in accuracy improvements from under 40% with pretrained models to around 90% with proposed generalized Tanimoto similarity measures.
